Beyond Worst-Case Online Algorithms via Input Subsampling

Siddhartha Banerjee ††thanks: School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853. Email: sbanerjee@cornell.edu. Supported by AFOSR grant FA9550-23-1-0068.    Tianle Jiang ††thanks: Department of Computer Science, Duke University, Durham, NC 27708-0129. Emails: kamesh@cs.duke.edu, tianle.jiang@duke.edu. Supported by NSF grant IIS-2402823.    Kamesh Munagala22footnotemark: 2
Abstract

We study whether classical competitive ratios survive input subsampling, when both the online algorithm and the offline optimum are evaluated on the same subsampled input. We consider the canonical problems of prophet inequalities and ski-rental. In these settings, for any single subsampling rate, the classical worst-case ratios remain unchanged. We ask a stronger question: can one adversarial input remain worst-case at two distinct rates p>qp>q?

For prophet inequalities, in the model where the policy knows the sampling rate and learns item survival online, every instance has competitive ratio strictly below 22 at one of the two rates, and we determine the tight simultaneous guarantee. For ski rental, in the fluid model where sampling scales the horizon, the answer depends on q/pq/p. Against adversarial distributions over horizons, one unrestricted randomized algorithm achieves a strict simultaneous improvement over e/(e−1)e/(e-1) for every distribution exactly when q/pq/p is below approximately 0.340.34. Requiring the algorithm to buy by the breakeven time lowers this threshold to approximately 0.310.31, showing that unlike classical ski-rental algorithms, buying later can provably help in this setting.

Our results therefore reveal a new form of beyond-worst-case fragility under input subsampling: instances that are worst-case at one rate need not remain hard at two rates simultaneously.

1 Introduction

Competitive analysis evaluates an online algorithm by comparing its performance with an offline optimum on a worst-case input. When an instance has a natural scale – the number of arrivals or the duration of its horizon – the adversary may choose a different hard input at every scale. Consequently, the classical competitive ratio can hide an important structural question: is a worst-case instance intrinsically hard, or is its hardness finely tuned to the scale at which it is evaluated?

We study this question through independent subsampling. Starting from a single base ‘adversarial’ input, we retain each item independently with probability pp, and evaluate both the online algorithm and the offline optimum on the retained input. This is a natural way to vary the effective scale of an online instance while changing it as little as possible: every item is treated symmetrically, and surviving items retain their values/relative order. At the same time, subsampling is milder than other perturbations that are known to improve online guarantees: unlike random-order models, it preserves relative order [13, 2], and unlike targeted removal, it does not selectively delete particular distributions or realizations [27, 30]. Moreover, its different scales are naturally coupled: for q<pq<p, a qq-sample can be obtained by further subsampling a pp-sample at rate q/pq/p.

The effect of changing scale can vary dramatically across online problems. At one extreme, some hard inputs are essentially self-similar under subsampling. Paging [5] gives a simple example. A standard hard distribution for randomized paging draws each request independently and uniformly from a set of K+1K+1 pages, where KK is the cache size. Independent subsampling at any positive rate leaves the retained requests independent and uniform. Hence the same hard distribution yields the classical HKH_{K} lower bound simultaneously at every sampling rate.11 1 More precisely, for any fixed finite collection of rates, a standard concentration argument yields a single sequence approaching the HKH_{K} lower bound simultaneously for the collection.

At the opposite extreme, hardness may rely on fine-scale regularity that random thinning disrupts. In binary prediction, the regret of follow-the-leader is exactly proportional to the number of lead changes [3], so highly regular sequences such as 0101​…0101\ldots are worst-case; random deletion quickly destroys this structure. Relatedly, Bernoulli sampling has been used to regularize fictitious play and leader-based dynamics [26].

Between these extremes lies the phenomenon studied in this paper. The worst-case competitive ratio may remain unchanged at every individual scale: once the sampling rate is fixed, the adversary can simply retune its instance and recover the classical lower bound. Nevertheless, the instances attaining this bound may themselves be scale-sensitive: no single base instance may remain nearly worst-case at two distinct sampling rates. In other words, classical competitive analysis can be scale-invariant even when its worst-case instances are not.

We investigate this phenomenon in two foundational online stopping problems whose classical hard instances depend delicately on scale:

  • •

    Prophet inequalities. An adversary chooses a sequence of independent nonnegative random variables. Under pp-subsampling, each variable is independently retained with probability pp, and both the online algorithm and the prophet are evaluated on the retained sequence. Here subsampling changes the effective number of opportunities while leaving the distributions of the surviving variables unchanged.

  • •

    Ski rental. An adversary chooses a base horizon BB. We use the continuous-time formulation, in which viewing the instance at rate pp scales its effective horizon to p​BpB. Thus the same underlying instance is evaluated at two different length scales.

For either problem, looking at one rate at a time reveals nothing new at the level of the classical competitive ratio: after the rate is fixed, the adversary can tune an instance to that rate and force the factor 22 for prophet inequalities [25, 33] or e/(e−1)e/(e-1) for randomized ski rental [20, 5]. We instead fix two rates p>qp>q and require the adversary to choose one base instance that is evaluated at both. Our central question is: Can a single instance be simultaneously worst-case at distinct scales?

Our results show that the landscape is subtler than either of the extreme examples above. For prophet inequalities, worst-case instances are fragile for every pair of distinct rates: at least one of the two induced instances must have competitive ratio strictly smaller than 22. For ski rental, by contrast, fragility and robustness are separated by a sharp threshold in the scale ratio ρ=q/p\rho=q/p.

Our viewpoint is closely related to smoothed analysis, which asks whether worst-case behavior survives a random perturbation of an adversarial input [34]; related perturbation-based viewpoints have also been studied in online learning and online algorithms [32, 4, 8]. The distinction is that smoothed analysis typically fixes a perturbation level and asks for the worst performance after perturbation. Our question concerns the stability of the worst-case instances themselves as the perturbation level changes. Indeed, at every fixed subsampling rate the worst-case competitive ratio in our two problems is exactly the classical one; the phenomenon appears only when we ask whether the nearly extremal instances at two different rates overlap. Thus subsampling serves not merely as a source of randomness, but as a way to expose scale sensitivity that the usual worst-case ratio at any single perturbation level necessarily discards.

1.1 Our results

We give a tight characterization of how worst-case instances behave across two scales for prophet inequalities and ski rental. In both problems, we fix two sampling rates 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1 and denote ρ=q/p\rho=q/p. The adversary must commit to one underlying base instance – or distribution over base instances – whose induced instances are evaluated at the two scales.

Prophet inequalities. We consider two input models. In the stronger revealed-subsequence model, the algorithm is given the surviving sequence of distributions before observing their values and runs the optimal online policy for that sequence; it does not need to know the sampling rate. In the weaker revealed-rate model, the algorithm knows the original distributions and the sampling rate, but does not know which variables survive the sampling. Our proofs focus on the weaker model, where we analyze the optimal dynamic program adapted to input subsampling, and the positive results we obtain directly extend to the stronger model, since revealing the surviving sequence only gives the stronger model more information.

For a base instance ℐ\mathcal{I}, let C​Rℐ​(r)CR_{\mathcal{I}}(r) denote the ratio between the prophet’s value and the value of the optimal rate-rr dynamic program. For any single sampling rate rr, we show that the classical factor 22 remains tight: there is an instance ℐr\mathcal{I}_{r} with C​Rℐr​(r)→2CR_{\mathcal{I}_{r}}(r)\to 2. We augment the standard two-item hard instance: now it consists of many deterministic unit values followed by a rare high-value, with parameters tuned so that the optimal algorithm is nearly indifferent between accepting a surviving unit value and waiting.

In contrast, when there are two different sampling rates p,qp,q, we prove

supℐmin⁡{C​Rℐ​(p),C​Rℐ​(q)}≤2−ρ⁡(1−ρ)2​(3−ρ)<2.\sup_{\mathcal{I}}\min\{CR_{\mathcal{I}}(p),CR_{\mathcal{I}}(q)\}\leq 2-\frac{\rho(1-\rho)}{2(3-\rho)}<2.

Thus, although the adversary can choose a different tight instance at each individual rate, no single base instance can be nearly tight at both rates simultaneously. More generally, we characterize the exact Pareto frontier between C​Rℐ​(p)CR_{\mathcal{I}}(p) and C​Rℐ​(q)CR_{\mathcal{I}}(q) for the weaker model, and give asymptotically matching instances.

Randomized ski rental. For classical ski rental (with unit buying cost, and unit per period rental cost), the optimal randomized competitive ratio is e/(e−1)≈1.58e/(e-1)\approx 1.58, achieved by the truncated-exponential equalizer distribution [20, 5]. This continues to hold for any single subsampling rate.

In contrast, we evaluate one buy-time distribution at the two scaled horizons p​BpB and q​BqB, where ρ=q/p<1\rho=q/p<1. The algorithm knows the scale ratio ρ=q/p\rho=q/p and chooses a single buy-time distribution that is evaluated at both horizons p​BpB and q​BqB. This allows us to ask whether the same adversarial input remains hard at both scales even when the strategy is chosen for that comparison. Already for a deterministic adversary choosing a single horizon BB, simultaneous hardness is fragile: by slightly perturbing the classical exponential buying distribution, the algorithm can concentrate its nearly worst-case performance into a narrow range of horizons. Since p​BpB and q​BqB differ by the factor ρ\rho, they cannot both lie in this range. Consequently, for every fixed ρ¯<1\bar{\rho}<1, there is an algorithm that obtains a uniform strict improvement over e/(e−1)e/(e-1) at one of the two scales whenever ρ≤ρ¯\rho\leq\bar{\rho}.

Our technically and conceptually more interesting results are for a distributional adversary, which chooses a probability distribution over base horizons.

In this setting, whether simultaneous improvement is possible depends sharply on ρ\rho. We obtain an exact threshold for each of two algorithm classes. Below the threshold, one algorithm achieves a uniform strict improvement: for every adversarial distribution, at least one of the two scales has competitive ratio smaller than e/(e−1)e/(e-1) by a fixed amount. At or above the threshold, every algorithm admits an adversarial distribution that prevents any strict simultaneous improvement. For algorithms constrained to buy by the breakeven time, this threshold is ρ⋆≈0.311\rho_{\star}\approx 0.311; for arbitrary algorithms, it is ρall≈0.338\rho_{\mathrm{all}}\approx 0.338. The existence of these thresholds and the gap between them are surprising and show that in this model, unlike classical ski rental, buying by the breakeven time is not without loss for distributional adversaries.

Finally, for distributional adversaries, we show that when the algorithm knows only an upper bound on ρ\rho, a single algorithm cannot obtain a uniform strict improvement over e/(e−1)e/(e-1).

Technical highlights.

In addition to the conceptual contribution, our paper involves several new technical ideas. At a high level, at each scale separately, classical competitive analysis gives exactly the same worst-case ratio, so the scalar ratio itself contains no indication of the simultaneous improvement. Our proofs therefore retain one additional layer of information – the signed slack in the classical tight guarantee – and study how this slack can trade off across two linked scales.

For prophet inequalities, the relevant slack is the difference between the online value and one half of the prophet’s value. We revisit the standard dynamic-programming proof and identify two losses that are normally discarded: replacing the changing continuation values by a common threshold, and upper-bounding the prophet’s maximum by a baseline plus the sum of excesses above it. An instance can make both losses small at one sampling rate, but not at two distinct rates simultaneously. A simple version of the argument uses two cutoffs to divide all instances into three cases and argue that in each case, some loss is large for pp or qq. This certifies an improvement below 22 that depends on ρ\rho. For the exact frontier, we refine this argument using the two continuation thresholds; independence reduces the remaining optimization to one over products of failure probabilities, yielding both the Pareto frontier and matching instances.

For ski rental, we study the residual curve: the difference between an algorithm’s expected cost and the target multiple of the offline optimum [19], viewed as a function of the horizon. The problem then reduces to two sets of conditions: conditions governing when a residual curve can be realized by a ski-rental algorithm, and the two-scale inequalities governing simultaneous improvement over ee−1\frac{e}{e-1}. We derive a necessary weighted-integral condition for realizability and a partial converse under the regularity conditions used in our constructions. For the impossibility results, we combine the two-scale inequalities with nonnegative weights and show that they contradict the necessary realizability condition. For the positive results, we construct residual curves that satisfy the two-scale inequalities and the sufficient realization conditions, recursively balancing positive residual at one scale with negative residual at a smaller scale. Strikingly, the same recurrence governs both the positive construction and the nonnegative weights in the impossibility proof, allowing the two arguments to meet at an exact threshold.

1.2 Related work

Random perturbations and beyond worst case. In addition to the smoothed analysis work cited above, another line of beyond-worst-case work augments the online algorithm with predictions, samples, or distributional advice. For example, Diakonikolas et al. [11] study online algorithms with distributional advice for both prophet inequalities and ski rental. These models, like ours, introduce information or structure beyond the realized online input, but the role of that information is different: our objective is to understand how one adversarial base instance behaves when viewed at two scales.

Prophet inequalities. The classical prophet inequality of Krengel, Sucheston, and Garling [25] shows that a gambler observing independent nonnegative random variables can obtain at least half of the expected maximum. Samuel-Cahn later showed that this guarantee can be achieved by a single-threshold rule [33]. Prophet inequalities have since been extended to richer feasibility constraints, including matroids and related mechanism-design settings [24], and are closely connected to simple auction mechanisms [6, 28].

Several recent variants study settings in which part of the input is removed or reordered before the online decision is made. Liu et al. [27] introduce a variable-decomposition framework and show that, for non-identical distributions, one can recover the optimal i.i.d.-prophet constant β≈0.745\beta\approx 0.745 after removing a small constant number of distributions chosen by the algorithm. Correa et al. [30] study residual prophet inequalities, where the top kk realized values are removed before the remaining sequence is observed online. A different source of randomness appears in the prophet-secretary model, which keeps every variable but presents them in uniformly random order [13, 2]. Random order permits guarantees strictly better than the classical factor-22 bound.

These models are closely related philosophically to ours, but perturb the input in different ways. Targeted removal may select particular distributions or realizations, while random-order models alter the arrival order. Independent subsampling instead removes every variable symmetrically and preserves the relative order of the survivors. More importantly, our objective is not merely to improve the guarantee after perturbation, but to ask whether one base instance can remain nearly tight at two different subsampling rates.

The i.i.d. prophet setting provides another important benchmark [18, 1, 9]. Work on i.i.d. prophets has also studied comparisons finer than the competitive ratio by characterizing the possible gaps between the gambler and the prophet [17, 18, 22]. Our use of the signed gap from the classical prophet guarantee is similar in spirit, though our goal is to control how this gap behaves simultaneously at two linked sampling rates.

Ski rental. Ski rental is one of the canonical examples in competitive analysis. The deterministic optimum is 22, and the optimal randomized competitive ratio is e/(e−1)e/(e-1). The optimal randomized algorithm uses the classical equalizer distribution for the buy time. This and related rent-or-buy problems were studied in [20, 19]; see also the textbook treatment of [5].

Ski rental has also been a central test problem for learning-augmented online algorithms. Purohit et al. [31] introduced ski-rental algorithms with machine-learned predictions and consistency–robustness tradeoffs. Gollapudi and Panigrahi [15] studied rent-or-buy algorithms with multiple experts, and subsequent work considered multi-shop and other variants with learned advice [35]. Related stochastic models include semi-stochastic ski rental [29], distributional predictions [10, 23], and prior-independent finite-horizon ski rental [16]. These works provide the algorithm with a predicted horizon, expert advice, samples, or information about the horizon distribution, whereas our model asks how one adversarial base horizon behaves under two linked scalings.

Alternative competitive objectives. Dinitz et al. [12] optimize expected competitive ratio subject to bounds on the tail of the realized competitive ratio. Their characterization produces non-monotone, discontinuous buying distributions on recursively scaled time intervals. This superficially resembles our alternating constructions, where the inequality at yy is coupled to the inequality at ρ​y\rho y. The objectives are nevertheless different: their setting admits buying by the breakeven time without loss, while in our distributional two-scale model allowing later purchases strictly enlarges the range of ρ\rho for which simultaneous improvement is possible.

Alternative performance measures for prophet inequalities and ski rental compare the expectation of the realized ratio (EoR) with the classical ratio of expectations (RoE) [14, 7]. In particular, Chen and Zhang [7] optimize the minimum of EoR and RoE for ski rental. Their two coordinates correspond to different performance measures applied to one horizon distribution, whereas ours apply the same competitive measure to one base instance at two different scales.

2 The Prophet Inequality

In the classical prophet inequality, a gambler sequentially observes independent, nonnegative random variables X1,X2,…,XnX_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{n} drawn from known distributions, with finite expectations. Upon observing the realized value of XiX_{i}, the gambler must immediately and irrevocably decide whether to accept XiX_{i} and stop, or reject it and continue. The classical theorem of [25, 33] states that the expected offline optimum is at most twice the expected reward of an appropriate online threshold policy, and this factor is tight, as we discuss below.

2.1 Subsampling model

We now study the same problem under independent subsampling. For r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1], let Sr⊆[n]S_{r}\subseteq[n] be the random subset obtained by retaining each item independently with probability rr. Define the subsampled prophet benchmark

OPT​(r)=𝔼⁡[maxi∈Sr⁡Xi].\mbox{OPT}(r)=\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i\in S_{r}}X_{i}\right].

The expectation is over both the realized set SrS_{r} and the values of the variables XiX_{i}. We set the maximum over the empty set equal to 00.

We consider two input models: In the stronger revealed-subsequence model, the online algorithm is told the realized subsequence SrS_{r}, and then runs the optimal online policy for this surviving sequence of distributions; we use v~​(r)\widetilde{v}(r) to denote its expected reward. For our proof, it is more convenient to analyze a weaker revealed-rate model where the online algorithm knows the subsampling rate rr but not the realized subsequence SrS_{r}. We use vi​(r)v_{i}(r) to denote the optimal DP value-function from the suffix i,i+1,…,ni,i+1,\ldots,n in this unrevealed-subsampling process, with vn+1​(r)=0v_{n+1}(r)=0, and satisfying the following recurrence:

vi​(r)=r​𝔼​[max⁡{Xi,vi+1​(r)}]+(1−r)​vi+1​(r).\displaystyle v_{i}(r)=r\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max\{X_{i},v_{i+1}(r)\}\bigr]+(1-r)v_{i+1}(r). (1)

The expected reward of the DP is v1​(r)v_{1}(r). Clearly v~​(r)≥v1​(r),\widetilde{v}(r)\geq v_{1}(r), because revealing SrS_{r} only gives the online algorithm more information. Hence any bound of the form OPT​(r)v1​(r)≤c\frac{\mbox{OPT}(r)}{v_{1}(r)}\leq c also holds, a fortiori, for the more natural revealed-subsequence model: OPT​(r)v~​(r)≤c.\frac{\mbox{OPT}(r)}{\widetilde{v}(r)}\leq c. We therefore focus on v1​(r)v_{1}(r).

We restrict attention to nontrivial instances, meaning that at least one XiX_{i} is positive with positive probability. For every r>0r>0, such an instance has v1​(r)>0v_{1}(r)>0. We measure performance by the competitive ratio

C​R​(r)=OPT​(r)v1​(r).CR(r)=\frac{\mbox{OPT}(r)}{v_{1}(r)}.

The classical prophet inequality says C​R​(1)≤2CR(1)\leq 2, and the factor 22 is tight; to see this, consider a hard instance where X1=1X_{1}=1 and X2=(1/ϵ)⋅Bernoulli​(ϵ)X_{2}=(1/\epsilon)\cdot\text{Bernoulli}(\epsilon) for some sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0. As we show below, the factor remains tight for every single subsampling probability rr.

Our objective.

Our goal is to understand whether this single-rate tightness can occur simultaneously at two different subsampling probabilities. Fix 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1, with scale ratio ρ=qp∈(0,1).\rho=\frac{q}{p}\in(0,1). For a given instance, we evaluate the two competitive ratios

C​R​(q)=OPT​(q)v1​(q),C​R​(p)=OPT​(p)v1​(p).CR(q)=\frac{\mbox{OPT}(q)}{v_{1}(q)},\qquad CR(p)=\frac{\mbox{OPT}(p)}{v_{1}(p)}.

The simultaneous ratio of the instance is min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)},\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}, because the algorithm is considered successful if it beats the classical bound at least one of the two rates. Thus the question is whether the simultaneous competitive ratio

supinstancesmin⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}\sup_{\text{instances}}\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}

is still equal to 22, as it is for each rate separately, or whether it is strictly smaller than 22 once the same instance must be evaluated at both rates. We prove the latter, and in fact characterize the tight value. Note that we allow p=1p=1; in other words, qualitatively, our result says that for any instance, and any random subset of that instance, cannot both simultaneously attain the worst-case competitive ratio.

2.2 Single-rate tightness

We first prove that C​R​(r)≤2CR(r)\leq 2 for every fixed rr using the DP formulation. The argument is analogous to the classical prophet-inequality proof for r=1r=1 (i.e., without subsampling). We give the full argument because its two sources of slack will be useful later.

Proposition 1.

For every fixed r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1], C​R​(r)≤2CR(r)\leq 2.

Proof.

Fix a subsampling probability r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1]. Let vi​(r)v_{i}(r) denote the optimal expected reward from the suffix Xi,…,XnX_{i},\ldots,X_{n} when each item survives independently with probability rr, with vn+1​(r)=0v_{n+1}(r)=0. The optimal threshold at item ii is the continuation value τi​(r)=vi+1​(r)\tau_{i}(r)=v_{i+1}(r), and the DP recurrence is

vi​(r)\displaystyle v_{i}(r) =r​𝔼​[max⁡{Xi,τi​(r)}]+(1−r)​τi​(r)\displaystyle=r\,\mathbb{E}[\max\{X_{i},\tau_{i}(r)\}]+(1-r)\tau_{i}(r)
=τi​(r)+r​𝔼​[(Xi−τi​(r))+].\displaystyle=\tau_{i}(r)+r\,\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\tau_{i}(r))^{+}]. (2)

In particular, vi​(r)≥vi+1​(r)v_{i}(r)\geq v_{i+1}(r), so every continuation threshold satisfies τi​(r)≤v1​(r)\tau_{i}(r)\leq v_{1}(r). Telescoping the recurrence gives

v1​(r)=r​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(Xi−τi​(r))+].v_{1}(r)=r\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\tau_{i}(r))^{+}]. (3)

To upper bound the value of the prophet, we use the following standard single-threshold relaxation.

Claim 1.

For every r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1] and every t≥0t\geq 0, if Mr=maxi∈Sr⁡XiM_{r}=\max_{i\in S_{r}}X_{i}, then

OPT​(r)=𝔼⁡[Mr]≤t+r​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(Xi−t)+].\mbox{OPT}(r)=\mathbb{E}[M_{r}]\leq t+r\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-t)^{+}]. (4)
Proof.

Indeed, pointwise,

Mr≤t+(Mr−t)+≤t+∑i∈Sr(Xi−t)+,M_{r}\leq t+(M_{r}-t)^{+}\leq t+\sum_{i\in S_{r}}(X_{i}-t)^{+},

and taking expectations gives the claim. ∎

Combining the telescoping identity (3) with the relaxation (4) at t=v1​(r)t=v_{1}(r) gives

OPT​(r)\displaystyle\mbox{OPT}(r) ≤v1​(r)+r​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(Xi−v1​(r))+]≤v1​(r)+r​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(Xi−τi​(r))+]=2​v1​(r).\displaystyle\leq v_{1}(r)+r\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{1}(r))^{+}]\leq v_{1}(r)+r\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\tau_{i}(r))^{+}]=2v_{1}(r).

Thus C​R​(r)=OPT​(r)/v1​(r)≤2CR(r)=\mbox{OPT}(r)/v_{1}(r)\leq 2 for every fixed subsampling probability. ∎

We next show that this bound is again tight for every fixed rate.

Proposition 2 (Single-rate tightness).

For every fixed r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1], there exists a sequence of instances such that C​R​(r)→2CR(r)\to 2.

Proof.

Fix r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1] and choose 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1. Consider an instance with two stages. The first stage consists of kk deterministic variables X1=X2=…=Xk=1X_{1}=X_{2}=\ldots=X_{k}=1; the second stage consists of one rare large variable ZZ, where

Z={1ε​r,with probability ​ε,0,otherwise.Z=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\varepsilon r},&\text{with probability }\varepsilon,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Under rr-subsampling, the expected value of the final variable from the algorithm’s perspective is

r​𝔼​[Z]=r⋅ε⋅1ε​r=1.r\mathbb{E}[Z]=r\cdot\varepsilon\cdot\frac{1}{\varepsilon r}=1.

Therefore, while processing the deterministic 11’s, the optimal DP is indifferent between accepting a realized 11 and continuing. More explicitly, the continuation value at the final stage is 11. At each preceding stage, the current deterministic variable either fails to survive, in which case the continuation value remains 11, or survives and offers a value equal to the continuation value. Working backward through all kk deterministic variables therefore gives v1​(r)=1v_{1}(r)=1.

We now calculate the prophet’s value. The event that ZZ both takes its large value and survives subsampling has probability r​εr\varepsilon. On this event, the prophet receives 1/(r​ε)1/(r\varepsilon). On the complementary event, the prophet receives 11 exactly when at least one of the kk deterministic variables survives. These events are independent, and the latter event has probability 1−(1−r)k1-(1-r)^{k}. Hence

OPT​(r)=r​ε​1r​ε+(1−r​ε)​(1−(1−r)k)=1+(1−r​ε)​(1−(1−r)k).\mbox{OPT}(r)=r\varepsilon\frac{1}{r\varepsilon}+(1-r\varepsilon)\bigl(1-(1-r)^{k}\bigr)=1+(1-r\varepsilon)\bigl(1-(1-r)^{k}\bigr).

Because r>0r>0, we have (1−r)k→0(1-r)^{k}\to 0 as k→∞k\to\infty. Thus, for each fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0,

OPT​(r)⟶2−r​εas ​k→∞.\mbox{OPT}(r)\longrightarrow 2-r\varepsilon\qquad\text{as }k\to\infty.

Sending ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 gives OPT​(r)→2\mbox{OPT}(r)\to 2. Since v1​(r)=1v_{1}(r)=1 throughout, it follows that C​R​(r)→2CR(r)\to 2. ∎

The construction places the online policy at an indifference point: a safe value 11 and the rare final value have the same continuation value. Changing the sampling rate breaks this balance. The next subsection makes this observation precise.

2.3 Exploiting slacks of the DP analysis

Decomposition of the slack.

Write vr=v1​(r)v_{r}=v_{1}(r) for convenience. The last step of the proof of Proposition 1 has two possible sources of looseness: we use the relaxed upper bound for OPT​(r)\mbox{OPT}(r), and we replace each 𝔼⁡[(Xi−τi​(r))+]\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\tau_{i}(r))^{+}] by the smaller quantity 𝔼⁡[(Xi−vr)+]\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{r})^{+}]. Therefore, we can decompose the gap between OPT​(r)\mbox{OPT}(r) and 2​vr2v_{r} into a threshold slack plus a prophet slack as follows:

2​vr−OPT​(r)=\displaystyle 2v_{r}-\mbox{OPT}(r)={} r​∑i=1n(𝔼⁡[(Xi−τi​(r))+]−𝔼⁡[(Xi−vr)+])⏟T​-​Slack⁡(r)\displaystyle\underbrace{r\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\tau_{i}(r))^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{r})^{+}]\right)}_{\operatorname{T\text{-}Slack}(r)}
+(vr+r​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(Xi−vr)+]−OPT​(r))⏟P​-​Slack⁡(r).\displaystyle+\underbrace{\left(v_{r}+r\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{r})^{+}]-\mbox{OPT}(r)\right)}_{\operatorname{P\text{-}Slack}(r)}. (5)

Both slack terms are nonnegative. Since τi​(r)≤vr\tau_{i}(r)\leq v_{r}, we have 𝔼⁡[(Xi−τi​(r))+]≥𝔼⁡[(Xi−vr)+]\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\tau_{i}(r))^{+}]\geq\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{r})^{+}] for every ii; hence each summand in the threshold slack is nonnegative. This slack measures the loss from replacing the DP thresholds τi​(r)\tau_{i}(r) by the single global threshold vrv_{r}. The prophet slack is nonnegative by Claim 1 and measures the loss from applying that relaxation. Thus, whenever vr>0v_{r}>0, the competitive ratio is

C​R​(r)=OPT​(r)vr=2−T​-​Slack⁡(r)+P​-​Slack⁡(r)vr.CR(r)=\frac{\mbox{OPT}(r)}{v_{r}}=2-\frac{\operatorname{T\text{-}Slack}(r)+\operatorname{P\text{-}Slack}(r)}{v_{r}}. (6)

Thus a strict improvement over 22 follows whenever at least one of the two slacks is at least a constant multiple of vrv_{r}.

The two slacks under subsampling.

The decomposition also explains why the tight instance from Proposition 2 works. The deterministic block has flat thresholds equal to 11, so the threshold slack on this block is zero. The rare final item contributes only r​εr\varepsilon to the threshold slack. Meanwhile,

OPT​(r)=1+(1−r​ε)​(1−(1−r)k),\mbox{OPT}(r)=1+(1-r\varepsilon)(1-(1-r)^{k}),

while

v1​(r)+r​∑i𝔼⁡[(Xi−v1​(r))+]=2−r​ε.v_{1}(r)+r\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{1}(r))^{+}]=2-r\varepsilon.

Therefore the prophet slack is (1−r​ε)​(1−r)k(1-r\varepsilon)(1-r)^{k}, which vanishes as k→∞k\to\infty. After sending k→∞k\to\infty and then ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, both slacks vanish and C​R​(r)→2CR(r)\to 2.

The same construction provides intuition of why two different rates cannot be simultaneously tight. First consider the tight instance at r=pr=p, but evaluate it at the lower rate qq, and write ρ=q/p\rho=q/p. At rate qq, the last-item continuation value is ρ\rho. Moving backward across the deterministic block raises the DP value from roughly ρ\rho to 11, while v1​(q)→1v_{1}(q)\to 1 and OPT​(q)→1+ρ\mbox{OPT}(q)\to 1+\rho. Hence C​R​(q)→1+ρCR(q)\to 1+\rho. In the decomposition, the prophet slack is asymptotically negligible, but the thresholds are no longer flat: in particular, v1​(q)>τk​(q)≈ρv_{1}(q)>\tau_{k}(q)\approx\rho. The resulting threshold slack satisfies T​-​Slack⁡(q)→1−ρ\operatorname{T\text{-}Slack}(q)\to 1-\rho.

Conversely, consider the tight instance at qq, but evaluate it at pp. Now the last-item continuation value is 1/ρ>11/\rho>1, so the online algorithm rejects all deterministic 11’s and v1​(p)=1/ρv_{1}(p)=1/\rho. The thresholds before the last item are flat, so the threshold slack is asymptotically zero. However, the static-threshold upper bound uses the baseline v1​(p)=1/ρv_{1}(p)=1/\rho, while the prophet often receives only a deterministic value 11 below this baseline. This creates prophet slack, and in normalized form P​-​Slack⁡(p)/v1​(p)→1−ρ\operatorname{P\text{-}Slack}(p)/v_{1}(p)\to 1-\rho.

2.4 A simple two-rate improvement

In this section, we turn the intuition about the two slacks into a quantitative bound and show that, for two rates, the better competitive ratio is strictly smaller than 22. The proof is intended to be simple and intuitive; the constants are not optimized.

Theorem 1.

For every finite instance and every 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1, with ρ=q/p\rho=q/p,

min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}≤2−ρ2​(1−ρ)27<2.\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}\leq 2-\frac{\rho^{2}(1-\rho)}{27}<2.
Proof.

Write vr=v1​(r)v_{r}=v_{1}(r) and τi​(r)=vi+1​(r)\tau_{i}(r)=v_{i+1}(r), as above. Fix a parameter δ\delta with 0<δ<(1−ρ)/20<\delta<(1-\rho)/2; we choose its value at the end of the proof. The nontriviality assumption gives vp,vq>0v_{p},v_{q}>0, so all ratios below are well defined.

At a high level, we distinguish between two cases. If vqv_{q} is close to vpv_{p}, then the single-threshold relaxation at the lower rate qq using vpv_{p} already improves the factor 22. If vqv_{q} is separated from vpv_{p}, we place a threshold TT midway between them. When there is little expected mass above TT at rate pp, the prophet often receives a value below TT, and this creates prophet slack at rate pp. When there is substantial mass above TT, the same instance creates threshold slack at rate qq. Thus either the two DP values are close and the lower rate improves, or they are separated and one of the two kinds of slack is large.

We now quantify these three possibilities.

Case 1: vq≥(1−δ)​vpv_{q}\geq(1-\delta)v_{p}.

Apply the single-threshold relaxation (4) at rate qq with t=vpt=v_{p}. This gives

For the second line, use q=ρ​pq=\rho p and τi​(p)≤vp\tau_{i}(p)\leq v_{p}, which follows from the monotonicity of the DP values in (2). Lowering the threshold can only increase the positive part. C​R​(q)≤1+ρ1−δ=2−1−ρ−2​δ1−δ.CR(q)\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\delta}=2-\frac{1-\rho-2\delta}{1-\delta}. (8)

vp−T=T−vq=Δ2>δ​vp2.v_{p}-T=T-v_{q}=\frac{\Delta}{2}>\frac{\delta v_{p}}{2}. (9)

2.5 The tight two-rate result

Theorem 1 used one global cutoff TT and only the total mass above it. That coarse summary establishes a gap below 22, while leaving information about the positions of the DP thresholds unused. The sharp analysis retains that information.

Specifically, we use the following survival-conversion function to compare the same collection of independent events at the two sampling rates.

Definition 1 (Survival conversion function).

For 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1, define Γq,p:[0,1]→[0,1]\Gamma_{q,p}:[0,1]\to[0,1] by

Γq,p(ϕ)=inf{∏i=1n(1−pθi):n≥1,θi∈[0,1],∏i=1n(1−qθi)≥ϕ}.\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)=\inf\left\{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-p\theta_{i}):n\geq 1,\ \theta_{i}\in[0,1],\ \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-q\theta_{i})\geq\phi\right\}.

We also set Γq,p​(0)=0\Gamma_{q,p}(0)=0.

For ϕ∈[0,1]\phi\in[0,1], define

f⁡(ϕ)=1+ρ−(1−ρ)​ϕ21−(1−ρ)​ϕ,g⁡(ϕ)=2−(1−ρ)​ϕ​Γq,p​(ϕ).f(\phi)=\frac{1+\rho-(1-\rho)\phi^{2}}{1-(1-\rho)\phi},\qquad g(\phi)=2-(1-\rho)\phi\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi).

The tight simultaneous competitive ratio is

ζ⁡(q,p)=maxϕ∈[0,1]⁡min⁡{f⁡(ϕ),g⁡(ϕ)}.\zeta(q,p)=\max_{\phi\in[0,1]}\min\left\{f(\phi),g(\phi)\right\}. (21)
Theorem 2 (Tight two-rate subsampled-prophet theorem).

For every finite instance and every 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1,

min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}≤ζ⁡(q,p)<2.\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}\leq\zeta(q,p)<2.

Moreover, for every 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1, there is a sequence of finite instances for which the left-hand side converges to ζ⁡(q,p)\zeta(q,p).

The supporting lemmas and the full proof appear in Appendix A.

Proof roadmap.

Write a=v1​(q)a=v_{1}(q) and b=v1​(p)b=v_{1}(p) for the algorithm’s values at the two sampling rates. We first show that ρ​b≤a≤b\rho b\leq a\leq b. We describe the position of aa in this interval by ϕ=b−a(1−ρ)​b∈[0,1].\phi=\frac{b-a}{(1-\rho)b}\in[0,1]. Thus ϕ=0\phi=0 when the two algorithmic values coincide, while ϕ=1\phi=1 when they have the largest separation allowed by the scaling inequality. The proof reduces every instance to this single parameter.

To bound the prophet’s value, we split each item relative to the continuation thresholds at rates qq and pp. The contribution above the higher threshold is controlled directly by the dynamic program. The remaining contribution lies between the two thresholds and is bounded by b−ab-a. Replacing each such contribution by an independent variable that is either 00 or b−ab-a can only increase their expected maximum. After this replacement, the relevant quantity is the probability that all these variables are zero.

At rate qq, the dynamic-programming recurrence makes the resulting product telescope and shows that this probability is at least ϕ\phi. The function Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} converts this statement into a lower bound on the corresponding probability at rate pp. Substitution gives C​R​(q)≤f⁡(ϕ)CR(q)\leq f(\phi) and C​R​(p)≤g⁡(ϕ)CR(p)\leq g(\phi). The first bound increases from 1+ρ1+\rho to 22 as ϕ\phi runs from 00 to 11, while the second decreases from 22 to 1+ρ1+\rho. Their unique crossing therefore bounds at least one of the two competitive ratios strictly below 22.

For tightness, the construction in Appendix A chooses middle-range events that attain the conversion bound Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p}, together with baseline and rare high-value items that make the preceding inequalities approach equalities. Hence the crossing value describes the exact frontier.

Figure 1 illustrates the curve (f⁡(ϕ),g⁡(ϕ))\left(f(\phi),g(\phi)\right) parameterized by ϕ\phi when q=0.4,p=0.5q=0.4,p=0.5. It can be interpreted as follows: for each point (x,y)(x,y) on the curve, any instance such that C​R​(q)=xCR(q)=x must satisfy C​R​(p)≤yCR(p)\leq y.

Thus the feasible region of (C​R​(q),C​R​(p))(CR(q),CR(p)) lies below the curve, which is strictly separated from the worst-case point (2,2)(2,2). The intersection of the curve with the line y=xy=x gives the global worst case for min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}. In this case, we have min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}≤1.95265\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}\leq 1.95265.

A closed-form corollary.

The exact value ζ⁡(q,p)\zeta(q,p) is given by the one-dimensional frontier above. The next corollary gives a simple closed-form upper bound depending only on the ratio ρ=q/p\rho=q/p. It is not always tight, but it is explicit and strictly improves the classical factor 22 for every q<pq<p.

Corollary 1 (Closed-form simultaneous bound).

For every finite instance and every 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1, with ρ=q/p\rho=q/p, we have

min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}≤B⁡(ρ):=ρ2−5​ρ+122​(3−ρ)=2−ρ⁡(1−ρ)2​(3−ρ)<2.\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}\leq B(\rho):=\frac{\rho^{2}-5\rho+12}{2(3-\rho)}=2-\frac{\rho(1-\rho)}{2(3-\rho)}<2.

The proof of Corollary 1 also appears in Appendix A.

2.6 Application to sequential posted pricing

The prophet formulation also has a standard interpretation in single-item auction design. Consider a seller with one item and nn asymmetric bidders. Bidder ii has value ViV_{i} drawn independently from a known absolutely continuous regular distribution FiF_{i} with positive density fif_{i}, finite optimal revenue, and a strictly increasing virtual-value function. Let φi​(v)=v−1−Fi​(v)fi​(v)\varphi_{i}(v)=v-\frac{1-F_{i}(v)}{f_{i}(v)} denote bidder ii’s virtual value. By Myerson’s lemma, the expected revenue of any truthful mechanism equals its expected virtual surplus. Thus the revenue of the optimal auction is the expected maximum nonnegative virtual value:

𝔼⁡[maxi⁡φi​(Vi)+],φi​(Vi)+=max⁡{φi​(Vi),0}.\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i}\varphi_{i}(V_{i})^{+}\right],\qquad\varphi_{i}(V_{i})^{+}=\max\{\varphi_{i}(V_{i}),0\}.

Sequential posted pricing mechanisms provide the corresponding online analogue. In a sequential posted pricing mechanism, bidders are approached in a fixed order and each bidder is offered a take-it-or-leave-it price. Under regularity, choosing a price is equivalent to choosing a threshold in virtual-value space. Thus, if we define Xi=φi​(Vi)+X_{i}=\varphi_{i}(V_{i})^{+}, then the optimal sequential posted pricing policy is the dynamic program for the prophet problem on the variables XiX_{i}; the continuation value vi+1v_{i+1} determines the virtual threshold, and the posted price is φi−1​(vi+1)\varphi_{i}^{-1}(v_{i+1}). This is the standard reduction between sequential posted pricing and prophet inequalities; see, e.g., [6].

We now allow bidder participation to fluctuate. Under rr-participation, each bidder independently participates with probability rr. The mechanism knows rr, and each bidder’s participation is revealed when that bidder is reached. Let REV​(r)\mbox{REV}(r) denote the expected revenue of the Myerson auction run on the realized participating subset, and let SPM​(r)\mbox{SPM}(r) denote the expected revenue of the optimal sequential posted pricing mechanism tuned to participation rate rr. In virtual-value notation,

REV​(r)=OPT​(r),SPM​(r)=v1​(r).\mbox{REV}(r)=\mbox{OPT}(r),\qquad\mbox{SPM}(r)=v_{1}(r).

Therefore the results above apply directly to the competitive ratio REV​(r)/SPM​(r)\mbox{REV}(r)/\mbox{SPM}(r).

Corollary 2 (Two participation rates).

Fix two participation rates 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1, and let ρ=q/p\rho=q/p. For every collection of bidder distributions satisfying the preceding assumptions,

min⁡{REV​(q)SPM​(q),REV​(p)SPM​(p)}≤ζ⁡(q,p)<2,\min\left\{\frac{\mbox{REV}(q)}{\mbox{SPM}(q)},\frac{\mbox{REV}(p)}{\mbox{SPM}(p)}\right\}\leq\zeta(q,p)<2,

where ζ⁡(q,p)\zeta(q,p) is the tight two-rate competitive ratio from Theorem 2.

Proof.

Apply Theorem 2 to the nonnegative virtual-value variables Xi=φi​(Vi)+X_{i}=\varphi_{i}(V_{i})^{+}. For each participation rate rr, the subsampled prophet benchmark OPT​(r)\mbox{OPT}(r) is exactly the expected Myerson revenue on the participating subset, while the DP value v1​(r)v_{1}(r) is exactly the revenue of the optimal sequential posted pricing mechanism tuned to rate rr. Thus

REV​(r)SPM​(r)=OPT​(r)v1​(r)=C​R​(r).\frac{\mbox{REV}(r)}{\mbox{SPM}(r)}=\frac{\mbox{OPT}(r)}{v_{1}(r)}=CR(r).

The stated inequalities are therefore immediate from Theorem 2 and Corollary 1. ∎

3 Simultaneous Competitive Ratio for Ski Rental

This section studies simultaneous competitive ratio for the ski-rental problem. We first state the model and the objectives. We then move to proving our results for adversaries that choose a deterministic horizon, as well as those that choose a distribution over horizons.

Our approach starts with the classical view of the optimal randomized ski-rental algorithm as an equalizer: it achieves the same competitive ratio for all horizons. Our question asks whether this balance can persist when the same base horizon is viewed at two related lengths, yy and ρ​y\rho y. To study this, we compare the cost of an algorithm at each horizon to the target competitive ratio and capture the gap via a residual curve. Against a deterministic adversary, it is enough for the residual to be nonpositive at one of yy and ρ​y\rho y for every yy. A distributional adversary can mix horizons before the two ratios are compared, so this pointwise approach no longer suffices. The resulting condition couples the curve at yy and ρ​y\rho y in a single inequality. This relation drives both our constructions and our impossibility proofs, first through simple bounds and then through the sharp thresholds.

3.1 Model and objectives

We first recall the ski-rental problem. A skier needs skis for an unknown horizon y≥0y\geq 0. Renting costs r>0r>0 per unit time, while buying costs b>0b>0 and permits free use thereafter. The skier learns the horizon only when it ends. Thus a deterministic online algorithm is specified by a buy time x∈[0,∞]x\in[0,\infty]: it rents until time xx and, if y≥xy\geq x, buys at time xx. Here x=∞x=\infty means that the algorithm never buys. Its cost at horizon yy is

cxb,r​(y)={r​y,y<x,r​x+b,y≥x,c∞b,r​(y)=r​y.c^{b,r}_{x}(y)=\begin{cases}ry,&y<x,\\ rx+b,&y\geq x,\end{cases}\qquad c^{b,r}_{\infty}(y)=ry.

The offline optimum knows the horizon in advance and either rents throughout or buys immediately. Its cost is therefore

OPTb,r​(y)=min⁡{r​y,b}.\mbox{OPT}_{b,r}(y)=\min\{ry,b\}.

The breakeven time is b/rb/r. Scaling costs by bb and time by b/rb/r, define the normalized horizon and buy time by y^=r​yb\widehat{y}=\frac{ry}{b} and x^=r​xb\widehat{x}=\frac{rx}{b}. Under this normalization, renting costs one per unit time and buying costs one. We henceforth drop the hats and write

cx​(y)={y,y<x,x+1,y≥x,c∞​(y)=y,c_{x}(y)=\begin{cases}y,&y<x,\\ x+1,&y\geq x,\end{cases}\qquad c_{\infty}(y)=y,

and

OPT​(y)=min⁡{y,1}.\mbox{OPT}(y)=\min\{y,1\}.

A randomized ski-rental algorithm is specified by a distribution over a buy time X∈[0,∞]X\in[0,\infty]. If FF is the CDF of XX, its expected cost at horizon yy is CF​(y)=𝔼⁡[cX​(y)].C_{F}(y)=\mathbb{E}[c_{X}(y)]. For y>0y>0, its pointwise competitive ratio is

C​RF​(y)=CF​(y)OPT​(y).CR_{F}(y)=\frac{C_{F}(y)}{\mbox{OPT}(y)}.

We write Rski=ee−1R_{\mathrm{ski}}=\frac{e}{e-1} for the classical optimal randomized competitive ratio.

Two-rate model.

In our model, the adversary now chooses a base horizon B≥0B\geq 0. We use the fluid approximation in which the random retained duration at rate pp is replaced by its law-of-large-numbers limit p​BpB. Clearly, if there is only one subsampling rate pp, it is impossible to do better than the classical competitive ratio of ee−1\frac{e}{e-1}, because the adversary can simply scale the input horizon by a factor of 1/p1/p.

Therefore, we consider two different subsampling rates 1≥p>q>01\geq p>q>0, so the two realized horizons are p​BpB and q​BqB. It is convenient to normalize the larger realized horizon by setting y=p​By=pB. Throughout this section we write ρ=q/p∈(0,1)\rho=q/p\in(0,1), and use the equivalent setting where the adversary chooses yy and the two realized horizons are yy and ρ​y\rho y.

For a deterministic adversary, the goal is to find one algorithm FρF_{\rho} and one constant η>0\eta>0 such that, for every y>0y>0,

min⁡{C​RFρ​(y),C​RFρ​(ρ​y)}≤Rski−η.\min\{CR_{F_{\rho}}(y),CR_{F_{\rho}}(\rho y)\}\leq R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta.

For a distributional adversary, the adversary chooses a probability distribution μ\mu over base horizons. The objective measures the ratio of expected costs

C​RF​(μ)=𝔼y∼μ​[CF​(y)]𝔼y∼μ​[OPT​(y)].CR_{F}(\mu)=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mu}[C_{F}(y)]}{\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mu}[\mbox{OPT}(y)]}.

For y∼μy\sim\mu, let ρ​μ\rho\mu denote the distribution of ρ​y\rho y. The goal is to find FρF_{\rho} and η>0\eta>0 such that every nondegenerate22 2 A distribution is nondegenerate if it is not concentrated at y=0y=0. μ\mu satisfies

min⁡{C​RFρ​(μ),C​RFρ​(ρ​μ)}≤Rski−η.\min\{CR_{F_{\rho}}(\mu),CR_{F_{\rho}}(\rho\mu)\}\leq R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta.

Several positive results below use algorithms whose buy times are supported on [0,1][0,1]. The impossibility results state their support and assumptions explicitly, and as we show later, unlike classic ski rental, a support on [0,1][0,1] is not without loss of generality in our case.

3.2 Residual curves and realization

Our analysis starts from the classic randomized ski-rental algorithm. It chooses a buy time in [0,1][0,1] according to the density f⋆​(x)=ex/(e−1)f^{\star}(x)=e^{x}/(e-1), with CDF F⋆​(x)=(ex−1)/(e−1)F^{\star}(x)=(e^{x}-1)/(e-1) on [0,1][0,1]. It is an equalizer: for every realized horizon yy, its expected cost is Rski​OPT​(y)R_{\mathrm{ski}}\mbox{OPT}(y) [20, 19, 5].

Since our goal is to beat RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}} in the two-rate model, we need to deviate from the equalizer. It is convenient to measure cost relative to an improved target. Given an algorithm FF and a target improvement η>0\eta>0, define its residual at ratio Rski−ηR_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta by

AF,η​(y):=CF​(y)−(Rski−η)​OPT​(y).A_{F,\eta}(y):=C_{F}(y)-(R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta)\mbox{OPT}(y).

Then at every realized horizon y>0y>0,

C​RF​(y)=Rski−η+AF,η​(y)OPT​(y).CR_{F}(y)=R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta+\frac{A_{F,\eta}(y)}{\mbox{OPT}(y)}.

Thus the target ratio is met at horizon yy exactly when AF,η​(y)≤0A_{F,\eta}(y)\leq 0. Since the equalizer is optimal in the classical setting, we cannot hope to achieve AF,η​(y)≤0A_{F,\eta}(y)\leq 0 at every horizon yy. Fortunately, this is also not required in the two-rate model: an algorithm only needs to achieve the target ratio for an appropriate subset of horizons. As we will show later, for deterministic adversaries, for each y>0y>0 the algorithm only needs to ensure that at least one of AF,η​(y)≤0A_{F,\eta}(y)\leq 0 and AF,η​(ρ​y)≤0A_{F,\eta}(\rho y)\leq 0 holds; for distributional adversaries, a stronger condition is needed.

In this section, we reduce designing ski-rental algorithms to designing the residual curve. First, we leverage the exponential distribution, which was used to prove the lower bound for classic ski-rental, to derive a necessary condition (Lemma 1) for what residual curves can be realized by a ski-rental algorithm. Next, we prove a weaker reverse direction: under mild additional conditions, every such curve can be converted back to a ski-rental algorithm that preserves a constant fraction of the residual at every horizon. Subsequent sections thus focus on showing possibility or impossibility of constructing a residual curve that simultaneously satisfies the condition in Lemma 1 and the additional conditions for ensuring a simultaneous competitive ratio better than RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}.

Necessary condition of residual curves.

For any measurable AA satisfying ∫0∞|A⁡(y)|​e−y​𝑑y<∞\int_{0}^{\infty}|A(y)|e^{-y}dy<\infty, define its exponentially weighted mass by

ℒ⁡(A):=e​∫0∞A⁡(y)​e−y​𝑑y.\mathcal{L}(A):=e\int_{0}^{\infty}A(y)e^{-y}dy.
Lemma 1 (Positive weighted mass).

Let FF be a randomized ski-rental algorithm, let R<RskiR<R_{\mathrm{ski}}, and let A⁡(y)=CF​(y)−R⋅OPT​(y)A(y)=C_{F}(y)-R\cdot\mbox{OPT}(y). Then ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0.

Proof.

Suppose the horizon yy is drawn from the distribution on [0,∞)[0,\infty) with density e−ye^{-y}. Then

∫0∞OPT​(y)​e−y​𝑑y=∫01y​e−y​𝑑y+∫1∞e−y​𝑑y=1−1e.\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{OPT}(y)e^{-y}dy=\int_{0}^{1}ye^{-y}dy+\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{-y}dy=1-\frac{1}{e}.

For any finite deterministic buy time x≥0x\geq 0,

∫0∞cx​(y)​e−y​𝑑y=∫0xy​e−y​𝑑y+∫x∞(x+1)​e−y​𝑑y=1.\int_{0}^{\infty}c_{x}(y)e^{-y}dy=\int_{0}^{x}ye^{-y}dy+\int_{x}^{\infty}(x+1)e^{-y}dy=1.

The same identity holds for x=∞x=\infty, since then c∞​(y)=yc_{\infty}(y)=y. Therefore, for any randomized algorithm FF, including one with arbitrary buying times, Tonelli’s theorem gives

∫0∞CF​(y)​e−y​𝑑y=𝔼X∼F​[∫0∞cX​(y)​e−y​𝑑y]=1.\int_{0}^{\infty}C_{F}(y)e^{-y}dy=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim F}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}c_{X}(y)e^{-y}dy\right]=1.

It follows that

ℒ⁡(A)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(A) =e∫0∞CF(y)e−ydy−R⋅e∫0∞OPT(y)e−ydy\displaystyle=e\int_{0}^{\infty}C_{F}(y)e^{-y}dy-R\cdot e\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{OPT}(y)e^{-y}dy
=e−R⁡(e−1)=(Rski−R)​(e−1)>0.∎\displaystyle=e-R(e-1)=(R_{\mathrm{ski}}-R)(e-1)>0.\qed

In particular, for the residual at target ratio R=Rski−ηR=R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta, ℒ⁡(AF,η)=(e−1)​η\mathcal{L}(A_{F,\eta})=(e-1)\eta. Thus a candidate algorithm must leave a positive amount of residual somewhere.

Realizing a residual curve.

We next give a partial converse to Lemma 1. For a candidate residual curve AA with positive weighted mass, define

ηA:=ℒ⁡(A)e−1,\eta_{A}:=\frac{\mathcal{L}(A)}{e-1},

and

ΦA​(y):=A⁡(y)−ηA​OPT​(y)+ey​∫0y(A⁡(x)−ηA​OPT​(x))​e−x​𝑑x.\Phi_{A}(y):=A(y)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(y)+e^{y}\int_{0}^{y}\bigl(A(x)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(x)\bigr)e^{-x}dx.

The function ΦA\Phi_{A} is the perturbation of the classical buying CDF corresponding to AA: under mild regularity conditions, F⋆+ε​ΦAF^{\star}+\varepsilon\Phi_{A} is a valid buying distribution whose residual is ε​A\varepsilon A.

Lemma 2 (Realizing a residual curve).

Let A:[0,∞)→ℝA:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be right-continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable with finitely many pieces and jumps. Suppose that A⁡(0)=0A(0)=0, ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0, and AA has a finite limit as y→∞y\to\infty. Suppose every jump of AA at or below time 11 is upward. Suppose also that there is a finite M≥0M\geq 0 such that ΦA′​(y)≥−M\Phi_{A}^{\prime}(y)\geq-M at every point y∈(0,1)y\in(0,1) where ΦA\Phi_{A} is differentiable, and that ΦA\Phi_{A} is nondecreasing on [1,∞)[1,\infty). Then, for every sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is a randomized ski-rental algorithm whose residual curve at target ratio Rski−ε​ηAR_{\mathrm{ski}}-\varepsilon\eta_{A} is ε​A\varepsilon A. If AA is constant on [1,∞)[1,\infty), the resulting algorithm is supported on [0,1][0,1].

The conditions in Lemma 2 have a direct interpretation in terms of the buying distribution. Below the breakeven time, the classical algorithm has strictly positive density, so sufficiently small bounded perturbations remain feasible; upward jumps of AA become positive buying atoms because ΦA\Phi_{A} has the same jumps. Above the breakeven time, the classical CDF is already flat at 11, so the perturbation ΦA\Phi_{A} itself must be nondecreasing. The proof and a few convenient admissibility checks are given in Appendix B.

3.3 Deterministic adversaries

We show that for deterministic adversaries, the simultaneous competitive ratio beats e/(e−1)e/(e-1), even if the algorithm only knows an upper bound α\alpha on ρ=q/p\rho=q/p, assuming α<1\alpha<1. This serves as a warm-up for our main results on distributional adversaries.

We first note that against deterministic adversaries, buying by the breakeven time is without loss of generality. The proof appears in Appendix C.

Lemma 3.

When the adversary chooses a deterministic horizon, restricting attention to randomized algorithms that buy by breakeven time is without loss of generality.

In the two-rate model, after the adversary chooses horizon yy, an algorithm is evaluated at both yy and ρ​y\rho y and it only needs to beat RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}} at one of them. Therefore, a residual curve at target ratio Rski−ηR_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta succeeds against a deterministic adversary whenever

min⁡{AF,η​(y),AF,η​(ρ​y)}≤0for every ​y>0.\min\{A_{F,\eta}(y),A_{F,\eta}(\rho y)\}\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }y>0.

This suggests a simple construction that places all positive residual inside a single interval that is narrow enough so that for any y>0y>0, the interval cannot contain both yy and ρ​y\rho y. Elsewhere the residual is simply set to zero.

Theorem 3 (Deterministic simultaneous improvement).

Fix α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). There exists a randomized ski-rental algorithm FF supported on [0,1][0,1], and a constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that for every 0<ρ≤α0<\rho\leq\alpha and every base horizon y>0y>0,

min⁡{C​RF​(y),C​RF​(ρ​y)}≤ee−1−ε.\min\{CR_{F}(y),CR_{F}(\rho y)\}\leq\frac{e}{e-1}-\varepsilon.
Proof.

Set ℓ=α/2\ell=\alpha/2 and u=1/2u=1/2, so that ℓ=α​u\ell=\alpha u. Let

A⁡(y)={κ​(y−ℓ)2​(u−y)2,ℓ<y<u,0,otherwise,A(y)=\begin{cases}\kappa(y-\ell)^{2}(u-y)^{2},&\ell<y<u,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

where κ>0\kappa>0 is chosen so that ℒ⁡(A)=e−1\mathcal{L}(A)=e-1. Then ηA=1\eta_{A}=1.

For any y>0y>0 and 0<ρ≤α0<\rho\leq\alpha, the two horizons yy and ρ​y\rho y cannot both lie in (ℓ,u)(\ell,u): otherwise ρ​y>ℓ=α​u>α​y\rho y>\ell=\alpha u>\alpha y, contradicting ρ≤α\rho\leq\alpha. Hence at least one of A⁡(y)A(y) and A⁡(ρ​y)A(\rho y) is zero.

We now check the conditions of Lemma 2. The curve AA is continuously differentiable, satisfies A⁡(0)=0A(0)=0, has no jumps, and converges to zero. Since ηA=1\eta_{A}=1, the derivative ΦA′\Phi_{A}^{\prime} is bounded below on (0,1)(0,1) because AA and A′A^{\prime} are bounded there. Moreover,

∫0∞(A⁡(x)−OPT​(x))​e−x​𝑑x=0,\int_{0}^{\infty}\bigl(A(x)-\mbox{OPT}(x)\bigr)e^{-x}dx=0,

because ℒ⁡(A)=e−1=ℒ⁡(OPT)\mathcal{L}(A)=e-1=\mathcal{L}(\mbox{OPT}). Since A⁡(x)=0A(x)=0 and OPT​(x)=1\mbox{OPT}(x)=1 for x≥1x\geq 1, for every y≥1y\geq 1 we have

ΦA​(y)=−1−ey​∫y∞(−1)​e−x​𝑑x=0.\Phi_{A}(y)=-1-e^{y}\int_{y}^{\infty}(-1)e^{-x}dx=0.

Thus ΦA\Phi_{A} is nondecreasing on [1,∞)[1,\infty), and all the conditions of Lemma 2 hold. It follows that there is a constant ε>0\varepsilon>0, possibly depending on α\alpha, such that ε​A\varepsilon A is the residual curve of an algorithm supported on [0,1][0,1] at target ratio Rski−εR_{\mathrm{ski}}-\varepsilon. Since at least one of A⁡(y)A(y) and A⁡(ρ​y)A(\rho y) is zero, this algorithm achieves the claimed simultaneous competitive ratio. ∎

3.4 Distributional adversaries: Preliminaries

We now move to our main results about distributional adversaries, where we show a sharp threshold of ρ\rho between possibility and impossibility of improving the competitive ratio. Further, unlike the deterministic case, buying by breakeven time is no longer optimal.

The distributional model uses the same residual AF,ηA_{F,\eta} as above, but the adversary may mix several horizons before the two rates are compared. For a deterministic horizon yy, the target ratio is achieved whenever AF,ηA_{F,\eta} is nonpositive at either yy or ρ​y\rho y. For a distribution over horizons, the analogous condition concerns the expected residual at the two scales. This distinction is the source of the additional difficulty.

3.4.1 Why distributional adversaries are harder

A distributional adversary can mix horizons that are bad in different ways. Recall that μ\mu is the distribution of the base horizon yy chosen by the adversary. An algorithm beats RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}} by η>0\eta>0 if and only if

min⁡{𝔼y∼μ​[AF,η​(y)],𝔼y∼μ​[AF,η​(ρ​y)]}≤0for every ​μ.\min\left\{\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mu}[A_{F,\eta}(y)],\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mu}[A_{F,\eta}(\rho y)]\right\}\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }\mu. (22)

For a deterministic adversary, the residual curve only needs at least one of AF,η​(y)A_{F,\eta}(y) and AF,η​(ρ​y)A_{F,\eta}(\rho y) to be nonpositive at every yy. The following example shows why the distributional condition (22) is stronger.

Suppose ρ=1/2\rho=1/2, and for some target improvement η\eta, the curve AF,ηA_{F,\eta} has values

AF,η​(1/4)=−0.1,AF,η​(1/2)=0.2,AF,η​(1)=−0.1.A_{F,\eta}(1/4)=-0.1,\qquad A_{F,\eta}(1/2)=0.2,\qquad A_{F,\eta}(1)=-0.1.

Then the deterministic condition holds at both y=1/2y=1/2 and y=1y=1. However, a distributional adversary can put probability 1/21/2 on y=1/2y=1/2 and probability 1/21/2 on y=1y=1, giving

𝔼y​[AF,η​(y)]=12​AF,η​(1/2)+12​AF,η​(1)=0.05>0,\mathbb{E}_{y}[A_{F,\eta}(y)]=\frac{1}{2}A_{F,\eta}(1/2)+\frac{1}{2}A_{F,\eta}(1)=0.05>0,

and

𝔼y​[AF,η​(ρ​y)]=12​AF,η​(1/4)+12​AF,η​(1/2)=0.05>0.\mathbb{E}_{y}[A_{F,\eta}(\rho y)]=\frac{1}{2}A_{F,\eta}(1/4)+\frac{1}{2}A_{F,\eta}(1/2)=0.05>0.

Thus the algorithm violates (22) and fails to beat RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}} against this distributional adversary.

3.4.2 A stronger condition from Farkas’ lemma

The above counterexample indicates that we need a stronger condition on the residual curve. We use the following special case of Farkas’ lemma.

Lemma 4.

Let V⊆ℝ2V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}. Exactly one of the following statements holds.

  1. 1.

    The convex hull of VV intersects ℝ>02\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}.

  2. 2.

    There exists a nonzero vector λ=(λ1,λ2)∈ℝ≥02\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{2} such that

    λ⋅v≤0for every ​v∈V.\lambda\cdot v\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.

In words, either c​o​n​v​(V)conv(V) intersects ℝ>02\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}, or there is a hyperplane passing through (0,0)(0,0) that separates it from ℝ>02\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}.

Lemma 5.

A residual curve A=AF,ηA=A_{F,\eta} satisfies (22) if and only if there exists γ>0\gamma>0 such that

A⁡(y)+γ​A​(ρ​y)≤0for every ​y≥0.A(y)+\gamma A(\rho y)\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }y\geq 0. (23)
Proof.

For brevity, write A:=AF,ηA:=A_{F,\eta} and R:=Rski−ηR:=R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta.

First suppose that AA satisfies (22). We begin with the endpoint y=0y=0. Let p:=Pr[X=0]p:=\Pr[X=0]. For every 0<y≤10<y\leq 1, the event X=0X=0 incurs cost 11, and hence

A⁡(y)=CF​(y)−R​y≥p−R​y.A(y)=C_{F}(y)-Ry\geq p-Ry.

If p>0p>0, then both A⁡(y)A(y) and A⁡(ρ​y)A(\rho y) are positive for all sufficiently small y>0y>0. Taking μ\mu to be the point mass at such a yy contradicts (22). Therefore p=0p=0, which implies CF​(0)=A⁡(0)=0C_{F}(0)=A(0)=0.

Now set

V:={(A⁡(y),A⁡(ρ​y)):y>0}.V:=\left\{\bigl(A(y),A(\rho y)\bigr):y>0\right\}.

Every finitely supported probability distribution on (0,∞)(0,\infty) is nondegenerate. Its expectation vector is a finite convex combination of points in VV, and every point in conv⁡(V)\operatorname{conv}(V) arises in this way. Hence (22) implies that conv⁡(V)\operatorname{conv}(V) does not intersect (0,∞)2(0,\infty)^{2}. Lemma 4 therefore gives λ1,λ2≥0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\geq 0, not both zero, such that

λ1​A​(y)+λ2​A​(ρ​y)≤0for every ​y>0.\lambda_{1}A(y)+\lambda_{2}A(\rho y)\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }y>0.

If AA is nonpositive on (0,∞)(0,\infty), then any γ>0\gamma>0 gives the two-scale inequality (23) directly. Otherwise both separating coefficients are positive. Indeed, if λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0, then A⁡(ρ​y)≤0A(\rho y)\leq 0 for every y>0y>0. Since ρ​y\rho y ranges over all of (0,∞)(0,\infty), this would make AA nonpositive everywhere on that interval. The case λ2=0\lambda_{2}=0 is similar. We may therefore divide by λ1\lambda_{1} and set γ:=λ2/λ1>0\gamma:=\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}>0, obtaining

A⁡(y)+γ​A​(ρ​y)≤0for every ​y>0.A(y)+\gamma A(\rho y)\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }y>0.

Since A⁡(0)=0A(0)=0, the same inequality also holds at y=0y=0.

Conversely, suppose that such a γ>0\gamma>0 exists that makes the two-scale inequality (23) true. We first verify that AA is bounded. For 0≤y≤10\leq y\leq 1, every deterministic buying time has cost at most y+1≤2y+1\leq 2, so CF​(y)≤2C_{F}(y)\leq 2 and AA is bounded on [0,1][0,1]. For t≥1t\geq 1, applying (23) at t/ρt/\rho and using CF​(t/ρ)≥CF​(t)C_{F}(t/\rho)\geq C_{F}(t) gives 0≥A⁡(t/ρ)+γ​A​(t)≥(1+γ)​A​(t)0\geq A(t/\rho)+\gamma A(t)\geq(1+\gamma)A(t). Thus −R≤A⁡(t)≤0-R\leq A(t)\leq 0 on [1,∞)[1,\infty), so AA is bounded there as well. Consequently, all expectations below are finite for every probability distribution μ\mu.

Taking expectations in the two-scale inequality (23) gives

𝔼y∼μ​[A⁡(y)]+γ​𝔼y∼μ​[A⁡(ρ​y)]≤0.\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mu}[A(y)]+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mu}[A(\rho y)]\leq 0.

The two expectations therefore cannot both be positive, proving (22). ∎

Combining Lemma 1 and Lemma 5 reduces the rest of our analysis to examining residual curves under the following two conditions:

ℒ(A)>0,A(y)+γA(ρy)≤0(y≥0).\mathcal{L}(A)>0,\qquad A(y)+\gamma A(\rho y)\leq 0\quad(y\geq 0).

We refer to the second condition as the two-scale inequalities. Positive results construct admissible residual curves satisfying both conditions, while negative results show that the two-scale inequalities force ℒ⁡(A)≤0\mathcal{L}(A)\leq 0. The following additional consequence is used repeatedly in the impossibility proofs.

Lemma 6 (Tail of a residual curve).

Let FF be a randomized ski-rental algorithm with simultaneous distributional competitive ratio at most R<RskiR<R_{\mathrm{ski}} at the two scales, and set A⁡(y)=CF​(y)−R​OPT​(y)A(y)=C_{F}(y)-R\mbox{OPT}(y). Then A⁡(t)≤0A(t)\leq 0 for every t≥1t\geq 1. Consequently, CFC_{F} is bounded, the algorithm buys eventually almost surely, and

limt→∞CF​(t)=𝔼⁡[X+1]<∞.\lim_{t\to\infty}C_{F}(t)=\mathbb{E}[X+1]<\infty.
Proof.

Set η=Rski−R>0\eta=R_{\mathrm{ski}}-R>0, so that A=AF,ηA=A_{F,\eta}. By Lemma 5, there exists γ>0\gamma>0 for which AA satisfies (23). Fix t≥1t\geq 1 and apply the two-scale inequality (23) at y=t/ρy=t/\rho. Both offline optima equal 11, and the cost curve CFC_{F} is nondecreasing, so

A⁡(t/ρ)=CF​(t/ρ)−R≥CF​(t)−R=A⁡(t).A(t/\rho)=C_{F}(t/\rho)-R\geq C_{F}(t)-R=A(t).

Therefore

0≥A⁡(t/ρ)+γ​A​(t)≥(1+γ)​A​(t),0\geq A(t/\rho)+\gamma A(t)\geq(1+\gamma)A(t),

which proves A⁡(t)≤0A(t)\leq 0.

It follows that CF​(t)≤RC_{F}(t)\leq R for t≥1t\geq 1, so the cost curve is bounded. For every buy time XX, the deterministic cost cX​(t)c_{X}(t) increases to X+1X+1 as t→∞t\to\infty, with the value +∞+\infty when X=∞X=\infty. Monotone convergence now gives limt→∞CF​(t)=𝔼⁡[X+1]<∞\lim_{t\to\infty}C_{F}(t)=\mathbb{E}[X+1]<\infty, which also shows that the algorithm buys eventually almost surely. ∎

3.5 Distributional adversaries: Main theorems

Our main result shows that the distributional model has a sharp phase transition in the scale ratio ρ\rho. There is a threshold value such that below it, one can beat the classical competitive ratio simultaneously, while above it every algorithm is stuck at the classical ratio. For algorithms that buy by the breakeven time, the threshold is ρ⋆≈0.311\rho_{\star}\approx 0.311. For arbitrary algorithms, the threshold is ρall≈0.338\rho_{\mathrm{all}}\approx 0.338.

Two aspects make our results interesting. First, feasibility turns out to have a sharp one-dimensional boundary in ρ\rho, even though the problems at different values of ρ\rho are not naturally nested: changing ρ\rho changes the two scales coupled by the two-scale inequality (23), and a construction for one ratio does not directly yield a construction for another. The threshold instead emerges from the common primal–dual recurrence underlying our proofs. Second, and more interestingly, there is a strict gap between these constants: buying by the breakeven time is not without loss of generality for distributional adversaries. The right panel of Figure 2 previews the extra freedom: an arbitrary algorithm can buy at a single time T>1T>1 with small probability.

Specifically, we show the following two theorems. The first theorem is proved in Appendix D, and the second in Appendix E.

Theorem 4 (Known ratio, buy by the breakeven time).

For a fixed ρ\rho, there exists a randomized ski-rental algorithm supported on [0,1][0,1] whose simultaneous distributional competitive ratio is strictly below e/(e−1)e/(e-1) if and only if ρ<ρ⋆≈0.311.\rho<\rho_{\star}\approx 0.311.

Theorem 5 (Known ratio, arbitrary algorithms).

For a fixed ρ\rho, there exists a randomized ski-rental algorithm with arbitrary buying times whose simultaneous distributional competitive ratio is strictly below e/(e−1)e/(e-1) if and only if ρ<ρall≈0.338.\rho<\rho_{\mathrm{all}}\approx 0.338.

To build towards these results, as a warm up, in Sections 3.5.1 and 3.5.2 we present simple versions of the positive and impossibility constructions and prove two suboptimal bounds. We then show in Section 3.6 that at ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, there is a separation between the two algorithm classes, and finally show in Section 3.7 that knowing ρ\rho is necessary to derive any improvement over e/(e−1)e/(e-1).

Proof idea.

At a high level, the positive and negative arguments are two sides of the same coin. As mentioned before, Lemma 5 shows that a successful residual curve satisfies (23) for some γ>0\gamma>0, while Lemma 1 shows that it must also satisfy ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0. For a positive result, we construct AA by making the two-scale inequalities (23) tight wherever possible: positive residual at one scale is canceled by negative residual at the next smaller scale, producing the oscillating pattern seen in Figure 2. For a negative result, we use the same inequalities in the opposite direction: we combine the two-scale inequalities (23) with nonnegative dual weights so that their sum controls the weighted mass of AA and make ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0 impossible.

Technically, the sharp thresholds are derived via refinements of the ideas presented for the warm-up settings in Sections 3.5.1, 3.5.2, and 3.6. In Lemma 8, we extend the dual-weight framework and upper bound ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) by a weighted integral that only depends on the tail of the residual AA after time 11. In Lemma 10 we present a general construction of the oscillating residual curve, which starts from a prescribed tail after time 11 and extends it recursively to earlier scales by making the two-scale inequalities tight. As the number of oscillations tends to infinity, the weighted mass of the resulting curves converges to exactly the same expression as the upper bound in Lemma 8. Thus the negative and positive arguments match symbolically: ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) can be made positive if and only if there is a residual tail that makes the expression positive. The remaining work in obtaining the sharp thresholds is therefore to determine for which regime of ρ\rho is this possible, and it turns out that there is a single threshold separating possibility and impossibility. The proofs use specific analytic properties of the dual weights that we verify using Lean.

This perspective also explains why buying by the breakeven time can be suboptimal in the two-rate model. If the algorithm buys by time 11, its residual is constant after time 11 and Lemma 8 would imply a stronger upper bound on ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A), while a general algorithm can induce a non-constant residual tail. We give a concrete illustration of the strict benefit of buying after the breakeven time for ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, where we show that constant tails cannot give positive weighted mass, while a linear tail corresponding to buying at time 33 does.

3.5.1 Simple possibility result for ρ≤1/10\rho\leq 1/10

We first present an algorithm whose simultaneous competitive ratio beats e/(e−1)e/(e-1) when ρ≤1/10\rho\leq 1/10. This serves to illustrate the first idea of using an oscillating residual curve, and the setting ρ≤1/10\rho\leq 1/10 keeps the number of oscillations small and the math simple.

Theorem 6.

Suppose 0<ρ≤1/100<\rho\leq 1/10. Then there is a randomized ski-rental algorithm, supported on [0,1][0,1], whose simultaneous competitive ratio is strictly smaller than RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}.

Proof.

We first work with a piecewise-constant curve and then smooth its downward jumps before applying Lemma 2. A0​(y)={0,0≤y<ρ2,−4,ρ2≤y<ρ,2,ρ≤y<1,−1,y≥1.A_{0}(y)=\begin{cases}0,&0\leq y<\rho^{2},\\ -4,&\rho^{2}\leq y<\rho,\\ 2,&\rho\leq y<1,\\ -1,&y\geq 1.\end{cases}

Hence A0​(y)+12​A0​(ρ​y)≤0A_{0}(y)+\frac{1}{2}A_{0}(\rho y)\leq 0 for every y≥0y\geq 0.

It remains to verify that ℒ⁡(A0)>0\mathcal{L}(A_{0})>0. Direct integration gives

ℒ⁡(A0)=−1+e⁡[2​(e−ρ−e−1)−4​(e−ρ2−e−ρ)].\mathcal{L}(A_{0})=-1+e\left[2\left(e^{-\rho}-e^{-1}\right)-4\left(e^{-\rho^{2}}-e^{-\rho}\right)\right].

ℒ⁡(A0)>5−3−32=12>0.\mathcal{L}(A_{0})>5-3-\frac{3}{2}=\frac{1}{2}>0.

Applying Lemma 17 with sufficiently small smoothing intervals, followed by Lemmas 2 and 5, gives a randomized ski-rental algorithm supported on [0,1][0,1] with simultaneous competitive ratio strictly smaller than RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}. ∎

We next give a simple impossibility proof for any algorithm when ρ\rho is sufficiently close to 11. The proof introduces the dual weighting argument that will also underlie the tight impossibility results.

Theorem 7.

3.6 Why buying after the breakeven time helps

The preceding bounds illustrate the main ideas behind the positive and negative arguments. We now extend these arguments to show that allowing purchases after the breakeven time strictly enlarges the set of scales ρ\rho admitting a positive result. Specifically, we show that at ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, every algorithm supported on [0,1][0,1] has simultaneous competitive ratio at least e/(e−1)e/(e-1), whereas an unrestricted algorithm can beat this competitive ratio.

The proof of this result serves to illustrate the additional analytic ideas and algorithmic constructions required for obtaining our tight results for both algorithm classes in Appendices D and E. Specifically, it illustrates the functional form of the weighted tail bound for the impossibility results, and the oscillating curve that arises from our dual function that leads to the possibility results.

3.6.1 A weighted tail bound and the function D⁡(ρ,ξ)D(\rho,\xi)

We start with a general lemma relating Uρ,ξU_{\rho,\xi} to the weighted tail ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A). This result holds more generally than the settings of ρ\rho we consider, and will therefore form the basis of our tight results in Appendices D and E.

Lemma 8 (Weighted tail bound).

Let 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, γ>ρ\gamma>\rho, and ξ:=ρ/γ∈[0,1)\xi:=\rho/\gamma\in[0,1). Let AA be a bounded measurable function satisfying (23). Suppose also that Uρ,ξ​(t)≥0U_{\rho,\xi}(t)\geq 0 for 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1. Then

ℒ⁡(A)e≤∫11/ρA⁡(y)​Uρ,ξ​(y)​𝑑y+∫1/ρ∞A⁡(y)​e−y​𝑑y.\frac{\mathcal{L}(A)}{e}\leq\int_{1}^{1/\rho}A(y)U_{\rho,\xi}(y)\,dy+\int_{1/\rho}^{\infty}A(y)e^{-y}\,dy. (31)
Proof.

For 0≤y≤1/ρ0\leq y\leq 1/\rho, we have ρ​y∈[0,1]\rho y\in[0,1], so the assumption gives Uρ,ξ​(ρ​y)≥0U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y)\geq 0. Multiply (23) by ξ​Uρ,ξ​(ρ​y)\xi U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y) and integrate over [0,1/ρ][0,1/\rho]. This gives

ξ​∫01/ρUρ,ξ​(ρ​y)​A​(y)​𝑑y+ξ​γ​∫01/ρUρ,ξ​(ρ​y)​A​(ρ​y)​𝑑y≤0.\xi\int_{0}^{1/\rho}U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y)A(y)\,dy+\xi\gamma\int_{0}^{1/\rho}U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y)A(\rho y)\,dy\leq 0.

Reorganizing and applying (30) gives

=∫01A⁡(y)​e−y​dy+ξ​∫11/ρUρ,ξ​(ρ​y)​A​(y)​dy≤0.\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}A(y)e^{-y}dy+\xi\int_{1}^{1/\rho}U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y)A(y)\,dy\leq 0.

ℒ⁡(A)e=∫01A⁡(y)​e−y​𝑑y+∫11/ρA⁡(y)​e−y​𝑑y+∫1/ρ∞A⁡(y)​e−y​𝑑y.\frac{\mathcal{L}(A)}{e}=\int_{0}^{1}A(y)e^{-y}\,dy+\int_{1}^{1/\rho}A(y)e^{-y}\,dy+\int_{1/\rho}^{\infty}A(y)e^{-y}\,dy.

Substituting (32) for the first integral gives

ℒ⁡(A)e≤∫11/ρ(e−y−ξ​Uρ,ξ​(ρ​y))​A​(y)​𝑑y+∫1/ρ∞A⁡(y)​e−y​𝑑y.\frac{\mathcal{L}(A)}{e}\leq\int_{1}^{1/\rho}\left(e^{-y}-\xi U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y)\right)A(y)\,dy+\int_{1/\rho}^{\infty}A(y)e^{-y}\,dy.

Applying (30) to the first integral completes the proof of (31). ∎

Specialization to buy-by-breakeven time algorithms.

We now specialize the above bound to buy-by-breakeven time algorithms. Previously we only used the property that A⁡(t)≤0A(t)\leq 0 for all t≥1t\geq 1. For algorithms that buy by the breakeven time, AA is actually constant on t≥1t\geq 1. This is because for t≥1t\geq 1, the algorithm’s and OPT’s cost are constant, which means A⁡(t)A(t) is a constant. This allows us to derive stronger impossibility and possibility results for this case.

Suppose that A⁡(y)=aA(y)=a for every y≥1y\geq 1. Then (31) gives

ℒ⁡(A)e≤a∫11/ρUρ,ξ(y)dy+a∫1/ρ∞e−ydy=a(∫11/ρUρ,ξ(y)dy+e−1/ρ).\displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{L}(A)}{e}\leq a\int_{1}^{1/\rho}U_{\rho,\xi}(y)\,dy+a\int_{1/\rho}^{\infty}e^{-y}\,dy=a\left(\int_{1}^{1/\rho}U_{\rho,\xi}(y)\,dy+e^{-1/\rho}\right). (33)

D⁡(ρ,ξ):=e​ξρ​∫ρ1Uρ,ξ​(x)​𝑑x,0≤ξ≤1.D(\rho,\xi):=\frac{e\xi}{\rho}\int_{\rho}^{1}U_{\rho,\xi}(x)\,dx,\qquad 0\leq\xi\leq 1. (34)

For the present argument ξ<1\xi<1, and the preceding calculation gives

ℒ⁡(A)≤a⁡(1−D⁡(ρ,ξ)).\mathcal{L}(A)\leq a\bigl(1-D(\rho,\xi)\bigr). (35)

Thus D⁡(ρ,ξ)D(\rho,\xi) is the coefficient produced by the dual weighting when the residual has a constant tail. Appendix D shows that the same quantity also governs the matching positive construction.

We now specialize to ρ=1/3\rho=1/3 and show the possibility and impossibility results. For 0≤ξ≤10\leq\xi\leq 1, write Uξ​(t):=U1/3,ξ​(t)U_{\xi}(t):=U_{1/3,\xi}(t). For 0≤ξ<10\leq\xi<1, (29) gives

Uξ​(t)=∑k=0∞(−ξ)k​e−3−k​t.U_{\xi}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-\xi)^{k}e^{-3^{-k}t}. (36)

At ξ=1\xi=1, U1U_{1} is given by the probabilistic definition in Lemma 7, or equivalently by the power-series extension in Lemma 18. At ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, the quantity in (34) becomes

The following lemma collects the three bounds needed for showing the separation between buy by breakeven time algorithms and general algorithms at ρ=1/3\rho=1/3. The first two make the dual certificate above valid and show that a constant residual tail cannot support positive weighted mass. The third shows that a suitable nonconstant tail can support this mass. Their generalizations in Appendices D and E yield the corresponding sharp thresholds for the two algorithm classes. We give machine-checked proofs in Lean for the second and third estimates, which also admit purely analytic proofs.

For every ξ∈[0,1]\xi\in[0,1],

3.6.3 Impossibility for buy-by-breakeven-time algorithms at ρ=1/3\rho=1/3

We now show that no algorithm supported on [0,1][0,1] can beat e/(e−1)e/(e-1) for simultaneous competitive ratio at ρ=1/3\rho=1/3.

Theorem 8 (Breakeven-time impossibility).

At ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, no randomized ski-rental algorithm supported on [0,1][0,1] can have simultaneous distributional competitive ratio strictly below RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}.

Proof.

Suppose that such an algorithm exists, and let AA be its residual at a target ratio below RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}. Lemma 1 gives ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0, while Lemma 5 gives some γ>0\gamma>0 such that (23) holds with ρ=1/3\rho=1/3. Since the algorithm is supported on [0,1][0,1], its residual is constant on [1,∞)[1,\infty); write A⁡(y)=aA(y)=a there. Lemma 6 gives a≤0a\leq 0.

If γ≤1/3\gamma\leq 1/3, Claim 2 gives ℒ⁡(A)≤0\mathcal{L}(A)\leq 0, a contradiction. Otherwise set ξ=1/(3​γ)∈(0,1)\xi=1/(3\gamma)\in(0,1). By Lemma 9, Uξ​(t)≥0U_{\xi}(t)\geq 0 on [0,1][0,1], so Lemma 8 applies. Using (35) and (38),

ℒ⁡(A)≤a⁡(1−Dξ)≤0,\mathcal{L}(A)\leq a(1-D_{\xi})\leq 0,

where the final inequality follows from a≤0a\leq 0 and Dξ<1D_{\xi}<1. This contradicts ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0. ∎

3.6.4 Possibility for general algorithms at ρ=1/3\rho=1/3

We now turn to unrestricted algorithms, and show that allowing AA to be nonconstant above 11 gives a positive result. The construction begins with a function on [1,∞)[1,\infty) and extends it recursively to earlier times. We first state the general form of this extension useful for our tight results.

Let 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, γ>ρ\gamma>\rho, and ξ:=ρ/γ\xi:=\rho/\gamma. The point now is that AA may vary after time 11 for general algorithms. The function gg specifies this tail, and (40) extends it to earlier times while preserving the two-scale inequality (23). The limit in (41) describes the resulting value of the weighted integral ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A). At ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, a suitable non-constant choice of gg makes this limit positive, while every constant tail gives a limit at most zero. This is the source of the benefit from allowing later purchases.

To show the positive result, we now apply the lemma with ρ=1/3\rho=1/3 and

g⁡(z)={z−4,1≤z<3,0,z≥3.g(z)=\begin{cases}z-4,&1\leq z<3,\\ 0,&z\geq 3.\end{cases}

The recursion constructs the function from larger times to smaller ones. Each new interval is a copy of the preceding one, compressed horizontally by 33, reflected across zero, and enlarged vertically by 1/γ1/\gamma. Figure 4 shows the first three pieces.

Corollary 3.

For every sufficiently large even NN, the function ANA_{N} satisfies (23) with AA replaced by ANA_{N} and ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, and ℒ⁡(AN)>0\mathcal{L}(A_{N})>0.

Proof.

The function gg is bounded and measurable, and g⁡(z)=z−4<0g(z)=z-4<0 for 1≤z<31\leq z<3. limN→∞N​ evenℒ⁡(AN)e=∫13g⁡(z)​Uξ​(z)​𝑑z=Iξ>0.\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\to\infty\\ N\text{ even}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mathcal{L}(A_{N})}{e}=\int_{1}^{3}g(z)U_{\xi}(z)\,dz=I_{\xi}>0.
