We can now realize one finite member of the sequence of ANA_{N} as an algorithm.

Theorem 9 (Strict benefit of late buying).

At ρ=1/3\rho=1/3, there is an unrestricted randomized ski-rental algorithm whose distributional competitive ratio is strictly below RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}. Every algorithm achieving such an improvement assigns positive probability to buying after the breakeven time.

Proof.

Fix a sufficiently large even NN as in Corollary 3. The function ANA_{N} is right-continuous and piecewise affine, has finitely many jumps, and its only jump above time 11 is the upward jump at time 33. Apply Lemma 17 to its downward jumps at or below time 11. As explained there, the smoothing can be chosen to give a curve A~N\widetilde{A}_{N} with ℒ⁡(A~N)>0\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{A}_{N})>0, while preserving the two-scale inequality (23) and leaving the tail unchanged:

A~N​(y)={y−4,1≤y<3,0,y≥3.\widetilde{A}_{N}(y)=\begin{cases}y-4,&1\leq y<3,\\ 0,&y\geq 3.\end{cases}

Lemmas 16, 2, and 5 therefore give an unrestricted algorithm with simultaneous competitive ratio strictly smaller than RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}. Theorem 8 shows that no algorithm supported on [0,1][0,1] can achieve such an improvement, while Lemma 6 shows that every improving algorithm buys eventually almost surely, hence buying after the breakeven time with positive probability. ∎

3.7 Unknown ρ\rho: Impossibility

We finally show that if only an upper bound on ρ\rho is known, then no single algorithm can beat the classical ratio against distributional adversaries for all sufficiently small ρ\rho.

Theorem 10 (Unknown-ratio distributional impossibility).

Fix α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). There does not exist a single randomized ski-rental algorithm and a constant η>0\eta>0 such that, for every ρ∈(0,α]\rho\in(0,\alpha], the algorithm beats RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}} by η\eta against every distributional adversary.

Proof.

Suppose such an algorithm FF and such an η>0\eta>0 exist. By decreasing η\eta if necessary, we may assume that R:=Rski−η>1R:=R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\eta>1. Let A⁡(y):=CF​(y)−R​OPT​(y),A(y):=C_{F}(y)-R\mbox{OPT}(y), and write a:=R−1>0a:=R-1>0.

We first locate a positive residual below the breakeven time. Fix any ρ0∈(0,α]\rho_{0}\in(0,\alpha]. Since the algorithm achieves the target ratio for ρ0\rho_{0}, Lemma 6 gives A⁡(t)≤0A(t)\leq 0 for every t≥1t\geq 1. On the other hand, Lemma 1 gives ℒ⁡(A)=(e−1)​η>0\mathcal{L}(A)=(e-1)\eta>0. Consequently there is a point y∗∈(0,1)y^{\ast}\in(0,1) such that M:=A⁡(y∗)>0M:=A(y^{\ast})>0.

For every admissible ρ\rho, Lemma 5 gives some γ=γ⁡(ρ)>0\gamma=\gamma(\rho)>0 for which AA satisfies (23). Every ski-rental algorithm has cost at least the offline optimum, so

A⁡(z)=CF​(z)−R​OPT​(z)≥−(R−1)​OPT​(z)=−a​OPT​(z)for every ​z≥0.A(z)=C_{F}(z)-R\mbox{OPT}(z)\geq-(R-1)\mbox{OPT}(z)=-a\mbox{OPT}(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\geq 0.

We will choose ρ\rho so small that the two inequalities become incompatible. Specifically, choose an admissible ratio satisfying

0<ρ<min⁡{α,y∗,M2a2​y∗}.0<\rho<\min\left\{\alpha,y^{\ast},\frac{M^{2}}{a^{2}y^{\ast}}\right\}.

First evaluate the Farkas inequality at y=y∗y=y^{\ast}. Since ρ​y∗<1\rho y^{\ast}<1, we have A⁡(ρ​y∗)≥−a​ρ​y∗A(\rho y^{\ast})\geq-a\rho y^{\ast}, and therefore

0≥M+γ​A​(ρ​y∗)≥M−γ​a​ρ​y∗.0\geq M+\gamma A(\rho y^{\ast})\geq M-\gamma a\rho y^{\ast}.

It follows that γ≥M/(a​ρ​y∗)\gamma\geq M/(a\rho y^{\ast}).

Next evaluate the same inequality at y=y∗/ρy=y^{\ast}/\rho. Now y∗/ρ>1y^{\ast}/\rho>1 and the scaled point is ρ​y=y∗\rho y=y^{\ast}, so A⁡(y∗/ρ)≥−aA(y^{\ast}/\rho)\geq-a and

0≥A⁡(y∗/ρ)+γ​M≥−a+γ​M.0\geq A(y^{\ast}/\rho)+\gamma M\geq-a+\gamma M.

Hence γ≤a/M\gamma\leq a/M. But our choice of ρ\rho gives M/(a​ρ​y∗)>a/MM/(a\rho y^{\ast})>a/M, a contradiction. ∎

4 Conclusion and Discussion

We view our results as a first step in understanding the robustness of worst-case instances for online algorithms. Several open questions remain. First, analogous to the prophet inequality result, what is the exact optimal simultaneous competitive ratio for ski rental as a function of ρ\rho? Our results locate the transition between improvement and impossibility, while the full performance curve below the threshold remains open. Second, how much information about ρ\rho does a ski-rental algorithm need? Intermediate models include a finite set of possible ratios or a short piece of advice.

The two problems also show that greater separation between the rates (that is, when ρ\rho is closer to 00) can have different effects on the simultaneous competitive ratio. For prophet inequalities, a block of values can be almost certain to survive at the higher rate but appear only rarely at the lower rate. The same block then provides a reliable choice at one rate and a rare prize worth waiting for at the other. The adversary can exploit this difference to make the competitive ratio approach 22 as the rates separate. For distributional ski rental, separation instead helps the competitive ratio. A buying strategy can accept higher costs at some horizons in exchange for lower costs at others, and sufficiently separated horizons allow this tradeoff to improve the guarantee at one of the two rates. When the horizons are closer, an adversarial distribution can prevent such an improvement. Understanding what determines these different responses to scale separation is a natural direction for further work.

More broadly, our work motivates the need to precisely identify structural conditions under which worst-case instances to online problems remain robust to subsampling and other random perturbations. Candidate problems include online bipartite matching, load balancing, and deterministic paging. Our ski rental results also show that the answer can depend on the separation between the two rates. For other problems, it could additionally be the case that the improvement or lack thereof depends on what combinatorial object is sampled. For online matching, the classical worst-case construction [21] suggests robustness under sub-sampling edges, but its fragility under vertex subsampling remains unclear. We leave such extensions as future work.

Generative AI Disclosure and Proof Verifier Use

The authors conceptualized the overall two-scale problem and proved the tight prophet inequality results and the simpler arguments presented in the main paper. We also conceptualized the distributional ski rental model. The proofs of the tight results for ski-rental were obtained via extensive conversations with GPT 5.6Pro, which also formalized some analytic lemmas in Lean. These conversations involved non-trivial inputs from the authors. We used Codex to help with the initial writing of the paper. We have kept the main paper intuitive and easy to understand via presenting results for special cases that convey the main ideas. For ease of readability and checking, we used Lean verification for certain analytic characterizations of the Uρ,ξ​(t)U_{\rho,\xi}(t) function (which otherwise involved tedious algebraic proofs). All content was verified by the authors who take full responsibility for this work.

Appendix A Proof of the Prophet Inequality Tight Result

Throughout the appendix, we fix 0<q<p≤10<q<p\leq 1 and set ρ=q/p∈(0,1)\rho=q/p\in(0,1). When defining variables that depend on pp, qq, or ρ\rho, we may therefore omit these parameters from the notation. Lower-case letters denote fixed values, while upper-case letters denote random variables.

We first establish two structural properties that compare the dynamic programs at the two sampling rates.

Lemma 11.

For every suffix ii, we have vi​(q)≤vi​(p)v_{i}(q)\leq v_{i}(p) and vi​(q)/q≥vi​(p)/pv_{i}(q)/q\geq v_{i}(p)/p.

Proof.

The first inequality is immediate from a coupling: an item that survives qq-subsampling can be viewed as also surviving pp-subsampling, while the larger rate may reveal additional items.

For the scaling inequality, we use backward induction. It is trivial for i=n+1i=n+1. Assuming it holds for i+1i+1, the recurrence gives

vi​(q)q\displaystyle\frac{v_{i}(q)}{q} =𝔼⁡[(Xi−vi+1​(q))+]+vi+1​(q)q,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{i+1}(q))^{+}]+\frac{v_{i+1}(q)}{q}, (44)
vi​(p)p\displaystyle\frac{v_{i}(p)}{p} =𝔼⁡[(Xi−vi+1​(p))+]+vi+1​(p)p.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-v_{i+1}(p))^{+}]+\frac{v_{i+1}(p)}{p}.

Since vi+1​(q)≤vi+1​(p)v_{i+1}(q)\leq v_{i+1}(p), the first expectation in the first line is at least the corresponding expectation in the second line; the induction hypothesis gives the same comparison for the second terms. Therefore vi​(q)/q≥vi​(p)/pv_{i}(q)/q\geq v_{i}(p)/p. ∎

A.1 Proof of Theorem 2

The proof associates each instance with a parameter ϕ∈[0,1]\phi\in[0,1] that measures the separation between its online values at rates qq and pp. We first split the prophet’s value into a part above the higher DP thresholds and a bounded part between the two collections of thresholds. Two lemmas control the bounded part by a product of failure probabilities. At rate qq, the DP recurrence makes this product telescope and produces ϕ\phi. The survival conversion function Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} then translates the same product bound to rate pp. This yields the two bounds C​R​(q)≤f⁡(ϕ)CR(q)\leq f(\phi) and C​R​(p)≤g⁡(ϕ)CR(p)\leq g(\phi), whose crossing gives the result.

It remains to control the expected maximum of the bounded random variables Iir​YiI_{i}^{r}Y_{i}. A.1.3 The lower sampling rate

We first apply Lemmas 12 and 13 at r=qr=q. Telescoping the qq-rate DP gives

di=v1​(q)−vi+1​(q)=q​∑j=1i𝔼⁡[(Xj−τj​(q))+]≥q​∑j=1imj.\displaystyle d_{i}=v_{1}(q)-v_{i+1}(q)=q\sum_{j=1}^{i}\mathbb{E}[(X_{j}-\tau_{j}(q))^{+}]\geq q\sum_{j=1}^{i}m_{j}. (55)

The inequality follows because the definition (45) gives mj≤𝔼⁡[(Xj−τj​(q))+]m_{j}\leq\mathbb{E}[(X_{j}-\tau_{j}(q))^{+}] for every jj. Substituting (55) into each factor in (51) yields

A.1.4 Transferring the product bound

To bound C​R​(p)CR(p), define the fixed numbers θi=mi/(b−a+di)∈[0,1]\theta_{i}=m_{i}/(b-a+d_{i})\in[0,1]. The proof of Lemma 13 established the stated range. Equations (57)–(59) give the product bound

∏i=1n(1−q​θi)≥ϕ.\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-q\theta_{i})\geq\phi. (61)

We now ask the following question: among all collections θi∈[0,1]\theta_{i}\in[0,1] satisfying (61), how small can the corresponding product ∏i=1n(1−p​θi)\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-p\theta_{i}) be? Define

Γq,p(ϕ)=inf{∏i=1k(1−pθi):k≥1,θi∈[0,1],∏i=1k(1−qθi)≥ϕ},\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)=\inf\left\{\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-p\theta_{i}):k\geq 1,\ \theta_{i}\in[0,1],\ \prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-q\theta_{i})\geq\phi\right\}, (62)

with Γq,p​(0)=0\Gamma_{q,p}(0)=0, as in Definition 1. Thus (61) immediately implies ∏i(1−p​θi)≥Γq,p​(ϕ)\prod_{i}(1-p\theta_{i})\geq\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi).

The collection giving the smallest product has a simple form: as many coordinates as possible are pushed to 11, at most one coordinate is fractional, and the remaining coordinates are 00. We give the exact formula because the same structure will later appear in the tight example.

Lemma 14.

For ϕ∈(0,1]\phi\in(0,1], choose an integer ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0 satisfying (1−q)ℓ+1≤ϕ≤(1−q)ℓ(1-q)^{\ell+1}\leq\phi\leq(1-q)^{\ell}. Then

Γq,p​(ϕ)=(1−p)ℓ​(1−1ρ​(1−ϕ(1−q)ℓ)).\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)=(1-p)^{\ell}\left(1-\frac{1}{\rho}\left(1-\frac{\phi}{(1-q)^{\ell}}\right)\right). (63)

In particular, Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} is continuous and nondecreasing on [0,1][0,1].

Proof.

First suppose p<1p<1. Let ui=1−q​θiu_{i}=1-q\theta_{i}, so ui∈[1−q,1]u_{i}\in[1-q,1]. Since p/q=1/ρp/q=1/\rho,

1−p​θi\displaystyle 1-p\theta_{i} =1−1ρ​(1−ui)=1ρ​ui−(1ρ−1).\displaystyle=1-\frac{1}{\rho}(1-u_{i})=\frac{1}{\rho}u_{i}-\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-1\right).

The right-hand side is increasing in uiu_{i}. Starting from any permitted collection with ∏iui>ϕ\prod_{i}u_{i}>\phi, we may therefore decrease one or more coordinates until the product equals ϕ\phi, without increasing the product we seek to minimize. If the existing coordinates reach the lower endpoint 1−q1-q before equality is reached, we append a coordinate initially equal to 11 and decrease it; repeating this operation reaches equality after finitely many steps because ϕ>0\phi>0. It therefore suffices to minimize under the equality constraint ∏iui=ϕ\prod_{i}u_{i}=\phi.

Write zi=−log⁡uiz_{i}=-\log u_{i}, let λ=−log⁡(1−q)\lambda=-\log(1-q), and let s=−log⁡ϕs=-\log\phi. Then zi∈[0,λ]z_{i}\in[0,\lambda] and the product constraint becomes ∑izi=s\sum_{i}z_{i}=s. Taking logarithms of the product reduces the problem to minimizing

∑ih⁡(zi),h⁡(z)=log⁡(1ρ​e−z−(1ρ−1)).\displaystyle\sum_{i}h(z_{i}),\qquad h(z)=\log\left(\frac{1}{\rho}e^{-z}-\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-1\right)\right).

The argument of the logarithm is positive on [0,λ][0,\lambda] because its minimum is the value 1−p>01-p>0 attained at z=λz=\lambda. A direct calculation gives

h′′​(z)=−1ρ​(1ρ−1)​e−z(1ρ​e−z−(1ρ−1))2<0,h^{\prime\prime}(z)=-\frac{\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-1\right)e^{-z}}{\left(\frac{1}{\rho}e^{-z}-\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-1\right)\right)^{2}}<0, (64)

so hh is concave.

Suppose two coordinates zi,zjz_{i},z_{j} both lie strictly inside (0,λ)(0,\lambda). Keeping zi+zjz_{i}+z_{j} fixed, the function t↦h⁡(t)+h⁡(zi+zj−t)t\mapsto h(t)+h(z_{i}+z_{j}-t) is concave on its permitted interval, so its minimum is attained at an endpoint. We may therefore move mass between the two coordinates until at least one reaches 00 or λ\lambda, without increasing the sum being minimized. Repeating this operation transforms every permitted vector into one in which all but at most one coordinate belong to {0,λ}\{0,\lambda\}, without increasing that sum.

The choice of ℓ\ell in the lemma is equivalent to ℓ​λ≤s≤(ℓ+1)​λ\ell\lambda\leq s\leq(\ell+1)\lambda. Hence the resulting vector has ℓ\ell coordinates equal to λ\lambda, one coordinate equal to s−ℓ​λs-\ell\lambda, and all remaining coordinates equal to 00. Substituting these values into the pp-rate product gives

Γq,p​(ϕ)\displaystyle\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi) =(1−p)ℓ​(1ρ​ϕ(1−q)ℓ−(1ρ−1))=(1−p)ℓ​(1−1ρ​(1−ϕ(1−q)ℓ)),\displaystyle=(1-p)^{\ell}\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\phi}{(1-q)^{\ell}}-\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-1\right)\right)=(1-p)^{\ell}\left(1-\frac{1}{\rho}\left(1-\frac{\phi}{(1-q)^{\ell}}\right)\right),

It remains to consider p=1p=1. If 0<ϕ≤1−q0<\phi\leq 1-q, choosing one coordinate θ1=1\theta_{1}=1 satisfies the constraint and makes the product zero. This agrees with (63), where one may choose ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. If 1−q<ϕ≤11-q<\phi\leq 1, then ℓ=0\ell=0 and s<λs<\lambda. No coordinate with θi=1\theta_{i}=1 can satisfy the constraint. For continuity away from zero, the explicit piecewise formulas agree at their common endpoints, including endpoints where either allowed choice of ℓ\ell may be used. Applying Lemma 13 with r=pr=p and using ∏i=1n(1−q​θi)≥ϕ\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-q\theta_{i})\geq\phi gives

𝔼⁡[maxi⁡Iip​Yi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i}I_{i}^{p}Y_{i}\right] ≤(b−a)​(1−Γq,p​(ϕ))=(1−ρ)​b​ϕ​(1−Γq,p​(ϕ)).\displaystyle\leq(b-a)\bigl(1-\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)\bigr)=(1-\rho)b\phi\bigl(1-\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)\bigr).

A.1.6 Completing the proof

The preceding arguments are summarized in the following lemma.

Lemma 15.

For every nontrivial instance, define a=v1​(q)a=v_{1}(q), b=v1​(p)b=v_{1}(p), and ϕ=(b−a)/((1−ρ)​b)\phi=(b-a)/((1-\rho)b). Then ϕ∈[0,1]\phi\in[0,1] and

C​R​(q)≤f⁡(ϕ),C​R​(p)≤g⁡(ϕ),CR(q)\leq f(\phi),\qquad CR(p)\leq g(\phi), (66)
Proof.

The range ϕ∈[0,1]\phi\in[0,1] was established after (59). The two bounds are exactly (60) and (65), including the endpoint ϕ=0\phi=0 handled there. ∎

The two bounds in Lemma 15 make the source of the simultaneous improvement explicit. The function ff is continuous and nondecreasing on [0,1][0,1]. Indeed,

f′​(ϕ)=(1−ρ)​(1−ϕ)​(1+ρ−(1−ρ)​ϕ)(1−(1−ρ)​ϕ)2≥0,f^{\prime}(\phi)=\frac{(1-\rho)(1-\phi)\bigl(1+\rho-(1-\rho)\phi\bigr)}{\bigl(1-(1-\rho)\phi\bigr)^{2}}\geq 0, (67)

while gg is continuous and nonincreasing because Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} is nonnegative and nondecreasing, and hence so is ϕ​Γq,p​(ϕ)\phi\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi). At the endpoints,

(f⁡(0),g⁡(0))=(1+ρ,2),(f⁡(1),g⁡(1))=(2,1+ρ).\displaystyle(f(0),g(0))=(1+\rho,2),\qquad(f(1),g(1))=(2,1+\rho).

Moreover, (67) is strictly positive for 0≤ϕ<10\leq\phi<1, while gg is nonincreasing. Hence the crossing point is unique. Since ϕ∗<1\phi^{*}<1 and f⁡(1)=2f(1)=2, its common value satisfies f⁡(ϕ∗)=g⁡(ϕ∗)<2f(\phi^{*})=g(\phi^{*})<2.

The crossing also gives the worst tradeoff. If ϕ≤ϕ∗\phi\leq\phi^{*}, then min⁡{f⁡(ϕ),g⁡(ϕ)}≤f⁡(ϕ)≤f⁡(ϕ∗)\min\{f(\phi),g(\phi)\}\leq f(\phi)\leq f(\phi^{*}). If ϕ≥ϕ∗\phi\geq\phi^{*}, then min⁡{f⁡(ϕ),g⁡(ϕ)}≤g⁡(ϕ)≤g⁡(ϕ∗)\min\{f(\phi),g(\phi)\}\leq g(\phi)\leq g(\phi^{*}). Therefore

ζ⁡(q,p)=maxϕ∈[0,1]⁡min⁡{f⁡(ϕ),g⁡(ϕ)},\zeta(q,p)=\max_{\phi\in[0,1]}\min\{f(\phi),g(\phi)\},

and the maximum is attained at ϕ∗\phi^{*} and is strictly smaller than 22.

Finally, every nontrivial instance has an associated parameter ϕ\phi, and Lemma 15 gives

min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}≤min⁡{f⁡(ϕ),g⁡(ϕ)}≤ζ⁡(q,p)<2.\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}\leq\min\{f(\phi),g(\phi)\}\leq\zeta(q,p)<2.

This proves Theorem 2. The construction below shows that this upper bound is tight.

A.2 Tight construction

The construction follows the equality conditions suggested by the proof. The last stage creates the single-rate indifference at the higher sampling rate. The middle stage realizes the extremal product in Lemma 14. The first stage then sets the low-rate baseline so that the algorithm is also indifferent there.

Fix ϕ∈(0,1]\phi\in(0,1], and let ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0 satisfy (1−q)ℓ+1≤ϕ≤(1−q)ℓ(1-q)^{\ell+1}\leq\phi\leq(1-q)^{\ell}. Define

θ\displaystyle\theta =1q​(1−ϕ(1−q)ℓ),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{q}\left(1-\frac{\phi}{(1-q)^{\ell}}\right), c\displaystyle c =1−(1−ρ)​ϕ.\displaystyle=1-(1-\rho)\phi.

The choice of ℓ\ell ensures θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1]. We construct an instance with three stages.

  • •

    Stage 1. There are NN deterministic variables, each equal to cc.

  • •

    Stage 2. There are ℓ\ell deterministic variables, each equal to 11, followed by a random variable WW with

    W={1,with probability ​θ,0,otherwise.W=\begin{cases}1,&\text{with probability }\theta,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
  • •

    Stage 3. There is one rare large random variable ZZ with

    Z={1ε,with probability ​εp,0,otherwise,Z=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon},&\text{with probability }\dfrac{\varepsilon}{p},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

    where 0<ε<p0<\varepsilon<p.

We take the limits first as N→∞N\to\infty and then as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

We first compute the DP values. Under pp-subsampling, Stage 3 has continuation value p​𝔼​[Z]=1p\mathbb{E}[Z]=1. Hence the algorithm is indifferent between accepting any realized value 11 in Stage 2 and waiting for Stage 3. The value entering Stage 2 is therefore exactly 11. Since c≤1c\leq 1, Stage 1 cannot improve this value, so v1​(p)=1v_{1}(p)=1.

Under qq-subsampling, the Stage 3 continuation value is q​𝔼​[Z]=q/p=ρq\mathbb{E}[Z]=q/p=\rho. The probability that no positive value from Stage 2 survives is

(1−q)ℓ​(1−q​θ)\displaystyle(1-q)^{\ell}(1-q\theta) =(1−q)ℓ​ϕ(1−q)ℓ=ϕ.\displaystyle=(1-q)^{\ell}\frac{\phi}{(1-q)^{\ell}}=\phi.

Thus the DP value upon entering Stage 2 is

(1−ϕ)⋅1+ϕ⋅ρ\displaystyle(1-\phi)\cdot 1+\phi\cdot\rho =1−(1−ρ)​ϕ=c.\displaystyle=1-(1-\rho)\phi=c.

The Stage 1 values are exactly cc, so the algorithm is indifferent throughout Stage 1 and v1​(q)=cv_{1}(q)=c.

We next compute the prophet benchmarks. Under qq-subsampling, the event that ZZ realizes its large value and survives has probability q​ε/p=ρ​εq\varepsilon/p=\rho\varepsilon. Since all earlier values are at most 11, for ε<1\varepsilon<1 the rare large value dominates whenever this event occurs. As N→∞N\to\infty, at least one Stage 1 value survives with probability tending to 11. Therefore, after taking the two limits in the prescribed order,

OPT​(q)\displaystyle\mbox{OPT}(q) ⟶ρ+(1−ϕ)⋅1+ϕ​c=1+ρ−(1−ρ)​ϕ2.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\rho+(1-\phi)\cdot 1+\phi c=1+\rho-(1-\rho)\phi^{2}.

Consequently

C​R​(q)\displaystyle CR(q) ⟶1+ρ−(1−ρ)​ϕ21−(1−ρ)​ϕ=f⁡(ϕ).\displaystyle\longrightarrow\frac{1+\rho-(1-\rho)\phi^{2}}{1-(1-\rho)\phi}=f(\phi).

For pp-subsampling, Stage 3 contributes asymptotic expected value 11. The probability that no positive Stage 2 value survives is (1−p)ℓ​(1−p​θ)(1-p)^{\ell}(1-p\theta). By Lemma 14 and our choice of θ\theta, this is exactly Γq,p​(ϕ)\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi). Hence

OPT​(p)\displaystyle\mbox{OPT}(p) ⟶1+(1−Γq,p​(ϕ))⋅1+Γq,p​(ϕ)⋅c=2−(1−ρ)​ϕ​Γq,p​(ϕ),\displaystyle\longrightarrow 1+\bigl(1-\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)\bigr)\cdot 1+\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)\cdot c=2-(1-\rho)\phi\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi),

while v1​(p)=1v_{1}(p)=1. Therefore

C​R​(p)\displaystyle CR(p) ⟶2−(1−ρ)​ϕ​Γq,p​(ϕ)=g⁡(ϕ).\displaystyle\longrightarrow{2-(1-\rho)\phi\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi)}=g(\phi).

Thus every ϕ∈(0,1]\phi\in(0,1] is asymptotically attainable on the frontier; the endpoint ϕ=0\phi=0 follows by taking ϕ↓0\phi\downarrow 0. Choosing a crossing point ϕ⋆\phi^{\star} maximizing min⁡{f⁡(ϕ),g⁡(ϕ)}\min\{f(\phi),g(\phi)\} gives instances for which

min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}\displaystyle\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\} ⟶ζ⁡(q,p).\displaystyle\longrightarrow\zeta(q,p).

This proves asymptotic tightness and completes the proof of the theorem.

A.3 Proof of the closed-form corollary

Proof of Corollary 1.

We next derive a closed-form upper bound that depends only on ρ=q/p\rho=q/p.

Set ϕ0=1−ρ/2\phi_{0}=1-\rho/2. For the parameter ϕ\phi associated with an arbitrary instance by Lemma 15, there are two cases. If ϕ≤ϕ0\phi\leq\phi_{0}, monotonicity of ff gives C​R​(q)≤f⁡(ϕ)≤f⁡(ϕ0)CR(q)\leq f(\phi)\leq f(\phi_{0}). If ϕ≥ϕ0\phi\geq\phi_{0}, monotonicity of gg gives C​R​(p)≤g⁡(ϕ)≤g⁡(ϕ0)CR(p)\leq g(\phi)\leq g(\phi_{0}). It therefore remains to compare g⁡(ϕ0)g(\phi_{0}) with f⁡(ϕ0)f(\phi_{0}).

We first lower-bound Γq,p​(ϕ0)\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi_{0}) without using its explicit piecewise formula. Couple the two subsamples by generating the pp-subsample first and then retaining each surviving item independently with probability ρ=q/p\rho=q/p. For any fixed collection of independent “success” events, conditional on at least one success surviving the pp-subsample, the probability that at least one of those successes remains after the additional ρ\rho-thinning is at least ρ\rho. Hence

Pr⁡[success under ​q]≥ρ​Pr⁡[success under ​p].\Pr[\text{success under }q]\geq\rho\,\Pr[\text{success under }p]. (68)

If the no-success probability under qq is at least ϕ0=1−ρ/2\phi_{0}=1-\rho/2, then the success probability under qq is at most ρ/2\rho/2. Equation (68) implies that the success probability under pp is at most 1/21/2, and therefore the no-success probability under pp is at least 1/21/2. By the definition of the conversion function, Γq,p​(ϕ0)≥1/2\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi_{0})\geq 1/2.

Consequently,

g⁡(ϕ0)\displaystyle g(\phi_{0}) =2−(1−ρ)​ϕ0​Γq,p​(ϕ0)≤2−(1−ρ)​ϕ02≤f⁡(ϕ0),\displaystyle=2-(1-\rho)\phi_{0}\Gamma_{q,p}(\phi_{0})\leq 2-\frac{(1-\rho)\phi_{0}}{2}\leq f(\phi_{0}),

where the last inequality is a direct algebraic simplification for 0<ρ<10<\rho<1. Thus in both cases min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}≤f⁡(ϕ0)\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\}\leq f(\phi_{0}).

It remains to evaluate f⁡(ϕ0)f(\phi_{0}). Since

1−(1−ρ)​ϕ0\displaystyle 1-(1-\rho)\phi_{0} =ρ⁡(3−ρ)2,\displaystyle=\frac{\rho(3-\rho)}{2},
1+ρ−(1−ρ)​ϕ02\displaystyle 1+\rho-(1-\rho)\phi_{0}^{2} =ρ⁡(ρ2−5​ρ+12)4,\displaystyle=\frac{\rho(\rho^{2}-5\rho+12)}{4},

we obtain

min⁡{C​R​(q),C​R​(p)}\displaystyle\min\{CR(q),CR(p)\} ≤f⁡(ϕ0)=ρ2−5​ρ+122​(3−ρ)=2−ρ⁡(1−ρ)2​(3−ρ)<2.\displaystyle\leq f(\phi_{0})=\frac{\rho^{2}-5\rho+12}{2(3-\rho)}=2-\frac{\rho(1-\rho)}{2(3-\rho)}<2.

This is the closed-form bound in Corollary 1. ∎

Appendix B Realizing Curves as Ski-Rental Algorithms

This appendix proves the residual-curve realization lemma used in the ski-rental results. The proof is based on an elementary identity for the expected cost of a buy-time distribution. It also records two simple admissibility tools used by the positive constructions: a tail calculation for late buying and a one-sided smoothing lemma for downward jumps.

B.1 General residual realization

For any buy-time CDF FF and any finite horizon yy, integration by parts gives

CF​(y)=∫[0,y](x+1)​𝑑F​(x)+y⁡(1−F⁡(y))=y+F⁡(y)−∫0yF⁡(x)​𝑑x.C_{F}(y)=\int_{[0,y]}(x+1)\,dF(x)+y(1-F(y))=y+F(y)-\int_{0}^{y}F(x)dx. (69)

Thus perturbing a buying CDF by a function Φ\Phi perturbs the cost curve by Φ⁡(y)−∫0yΦ⁡(x)​𝑑x\Phi(y)-\int_{0}^{y}\Phi(x)dx. The definition of ΦA\Phi_{A} in the main text is exactly the inverse of this relation.

Proof of Lemma 2.

Recall that

ηA=ℒ⁡(A)e−1\eta_{A}=\frac{\mathcal{L}(A)}{e-1}

and

ΦA​(y)=A⁡(y)−ηA​OPT​(y)+ey​∫0y(A⁡(x)−ηA​OPT​(x))​e−x​𝑑x.\Phi_{A}(y)=A(y)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(y)+e^{y}\int_{0}^{y}\bigl(A(x)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(x)\bigr)e^{-x}dx.

=∫0y(A⁡(x)−ηA​OPT​(x))​𝑑x+∫0y(ey−ex)​(A⁡(x)−ηA​OPT​(x))​e−x​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{y}\bigl(A(x)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(x)\bigr)dx+\int_{0}^{y}(e^{y}-e^{x})\bigl(A(x)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(x)\bigr)e^{-x}dx
=ey​∫0y(A⁡(x)−ηA​OPT​(x))​e−x​dx.\displaystyle=e^{y}\int_{0}^{y}\bigl(A(x)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(x)\bigr)e^{-x}dx.

ΦA​(y)−∫0yΦA​(x)​𝑑x=A⁡(y)−ηA​OPT​(y).\Phi_{A}(y)-\int_{0}^{y}\Phi_{A}(x)dx=A(y)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(y). (71)

Let F⋆F^{\star} be the classical equalizer CDF,

F⋆​(y)={ey−1e−1,0≤y≤1,1,y≥1,F^{\star}(y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{e^{y}-1}{e-1},&0\leq y\leq 1,\\ 1,&y\geq 1,\end{cases}

Fε​(y):=F⋆​(y)+ε​ΦA​(y).F_{\varepsilon}(y):=F^{\star}(y)+\varepsilon\Phi_{A}(y).

CFε​(y)−CF⋆​(y)=ε⁡(ΦA​(y)−∫0yΦA​(x)​𝑑x)=ε⁡(A⁡(y)−ηA​OPT​(y)).C_{F_{\varepsilon}}(y)-C_{F^{\star}}(y)=\varepsilon\left(\Phi_{A}(y)-\int_{0}^{y}\Phi_{A}(x)dx\right)=\varepsilon\bigl(A(y)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(y)\bigr).

CFε​(y)=(Rski−ε​ηA)​OPT​(y)+ε​A​(y),C_{F_{\varepsilon}}(y)=\bigl(R_{\mathrm{ski}}-\varepsilon\eta_{A}\bigr)\mbox{OPT}(y)+\varepsilon A(y),

so the residual at target ratio Rski−ε​ηAR_{\mathrm{ski}}-\varepsilon\eta_{A} is exactly ε​A\varepsilon A.

It remains to verify that FεF_{\varepsilon} is a CDF for sufficiently small ε\varepsilon. We have ΦA​(0)=0\Phi_{A}(0)=0. Using (70), we may also write

ΦA​(y)=A⁡(y)−ηA​OPT​(y)−ey​∫y∞(A⁡(x)−ηA​OPT​(x))​e−x​𝑑x.\Phi_{A}(y)=A(y)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(y)-e^{y}\int_{y}^{\infty}\bigl(A(x)-\eta_{A}\mbox{OPT}(x)\bigr)e^{-x}dx. (72)

The integral term in the definition of ΦA\Phi_{A} is continuous, as is OPT, so every jump of ΦA\Phi_{A} is exactly the corresponding jump of AA. In particular, all jumps at or below time 11 are nonnegative. On a smooth piece below time 11,

ΦA′​(y)=ΦA​(y)+A′​(y)−ηA.\Phi_{A}^{\prime}(y)=\Phi_{A}(y)+A^{\prime}(y)-\eta_{A}.

Because there are finitely many pieces and by the assumptions of the lemma statement, ΦA′\Phi_{A}^{\prime} is bounded below on (0,1)(0,1). Hence

Fε′​(y)=eye−1+ε​ΦA′​(y)≥0F_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}(y)=\frac{e^{y}}{e-1}+\varepsilon\Phi_{A}^{\prime}(y)\geq 0

for sufficiently small ε\varepsilon. On [1,∞)[1,\infty), F⋆F^{\star} is constant and ΦA\Phi_{A} is nondecreasing by hypothesis. Thus FεF_{\varepsilon} is a valid CDF.

Finally, if AA is constant on [1,∞)[1,\infty), then for y≥1y\geq 1 Equation (72) gives ΦA​(y)=0\Phi_{A}(y)=0. Hence Fε​(y)=F⋆​(y)=1F_{\varepsilon}(y)=F^{\star}(y)=1 for every y≥1y\geq 1, so the realized algorithm is supported on [0,1][0,1]. ∎

B.2 Admissibility checks

The tail form (72) simplifies further after the breakeven time. Since OPT​(x)=1\mbox{OPT}(x)=1 for x≥1x\geq 1, the ηA\eta_{A} terms cancel and

ΦA​(y)=A⁡(y)−ey​∫y∞A⁡(x)​e−x​𝑑x,y≥1.\Phi_{A}(y)=A(y)-e^{y}\int_{y}^{\infty}A(x)e^{-x}dx,\qquad y\geq 1. (73)

Thus the realizability of a nonconstant tail can be checked directly from AA, independently of the improvement ηA\eta_{A}. In particular, a constant tail gives ΦA=0\Phi_{A}=0 and hence a buy-by-breakeven-time algorithm.

The unrestricted positive constructions use the following simple nonconstant tail.

Lemma 16 (Tail check for the late-buying construction).

Let T>1T>1, and suppose a candidate residual curve AA has

A⁡(y)={y−T−1,1≤y<T,0,y≥T.A(y)=\begin{cases}y-T-1,&1\leq y<T,\\ 0,&y\geq T.\end{cases}

Then ΦA​(y)=−1\Phi_{A}(y)=-1 for 1≤y<T1\leq y<T and ΦA​(y)=0\Phi_{A}(y)=0 for y≥Ty\geq T. Consequently, ΦA\Phi_{A} is nondecreasing on [1,∞)[1,\infty), with a single upward jump of size one at TT.

Proof.

For 1≤y<T1\leq y<T, Equation (73) gives

ΦA​(y)=y−T−1−ey​∫yT(x−T−1)​e−x​𝑑x=−1.\Phi_{A}(y)=y-T-1-e^{y}\int_{y}^{T}(x-T-1)e^{-x}dx=-1.

For y≥Ty\geq T, both terms in (73) are zero. Thus ΦA\Phi_{A} is constant on (1,T)(1,T) and (T,∞)(T,\infty) and has an upward jump of size one at TT. ∎

B.3 One-sided smoothing

The constructions below are easiest to describe using piecewise-defined residual curves, which may initially have downward jumps. Since ΦA\Phi_{A} has exactly the same jumps as AA, a downward jump would require a negative buying atom. The smoothing lemma below replaces each downward jump by a short continuous transition. Since the smoothing only lowers AA, it preserves the two-scale inequality (23), while weighted convergence preserves positivity of ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) for sufficiently short smoothing intervals.

Lemma 17 (One-sided smoothing of downward jumps).

Let AA be a right-continuous, piecewise continuously differentiable function with finitely many pieces and jumps, and suppose that AA satisfies (23) for some γ>0\gamma>0. Let

ℬ−:={b>0:A⁡(b−)>A⁡(b)}\mathcal{B}_{-}:=\{b>0:A(b^{-})>A(b)\}

be its finite set of downward jumps, and write Δb:=A⁡(b−)−A⁡(b)>0\Delta_{b}:=A(b^{-})-A(b)>0. Then, for every sufficiently small δ>0\delta>0, there is a right-continuous function AδA_{\delta} such that:

  1. 1.

    Aδ≤AA_{\delta}\leq A pointwise;

  2. 2.

    AδA_{\delta} has no downward jumps;

  3. 3.

    Aδ=AA_{\delta}=A outside left neighborhoods of the points in ℬ−\mathcal{B}_{-} whose total length tends to zero with δ\delta;

  4. 4.

    AδA_{\delta} satisfies (23) with AA replaced by AδA_{\delta};

  5. 5.

    for every integrable nonnegative weight ww,

    ∫0∞|Aδ​(y)−A⁡(y)|​w​(y)​𝑑y⟶0(δ↓0).\int_{0}^{\infty}|A_{\delta}(y)-A(y)|w(y)dy\longrightarrow 0\qquad(\delta\downarrow 0).
Proof.

Choose a continuously differentiable nondecreasing function χ:[0,1]→[0,1]\chi:[0,1]\to[0,1] with χ⁡(0)=0\chi(0)=0 and χ⁡(1)=1\chi(1)=1. Choose δ\delta small enough that the intervals

Jb=[b⁡(1−δ),b],b∈ℬ−,J_{b}=[b(1-\delta),b],\qquad b\in\mathcal{B}_{-},

are pairwise disjoint and contain no jumps of AA except their right endpoints. Define Aδ=AA_{\delta}=A outside the interiors of these intervals, and for y∈[b⁡(1−δ),b)y\in[b(1-\delta),b) set

Aδ​(y)=A⁡(y)−Δb​χ​(y−b⁡(1−δ)b​δ).A_{\delta}(y)=A(y)-\Delta_{b}\chi\left(\frac{y-b(1-\delta)}{b\delta}\right).

At the lower endpoint of JbJ_{b} the correction is zero. At the upper endpoint,

limy↑bAδ​(y)=A⁡(b−)−Δb=A⁡(b),\lim_{y\uparrow b}A_{\delta}(y)=A(b^{-})-\Delta_{b}=A(b),

so the downward jump at bb is replaced by a continuous transition. Since all downward jumps are treated and no other jumps are introduced, AδA_{\delta} has no downward jumps.

Every correction is nonnegative, so Aδ≤AA_{\delta}\leq A. Therefore

Aδ​(y)+γ​Aδ​(ρ​y)≤A⁡(y)+γ​A​(ρ​y)≤0.A_{\delta}(y)+\gamma A_{\delta}(\rho y)\leq A(y)+\gamma A(\rho y)\leq 0.

Finally,

0≤A⁡(y)−Aδ​(y)≤∑b∈ℬ−Δb​𝟏Jb​(y).0\leq A(y)-A_{\delta}(y)\leq\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{-}}\Delta_{b}\mathbf{1}_{J_{b}}(y).

The intervals JbJ_{b} shrink to finitely many points as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0. The absolute continuity of the Lebesgue integral for the integrable weight ww gives the claimed convergence. ∎

Appendix C Deterministic Adversaries and Buy-by-Breakeven Time

In this section we give a formal proof for the assertion in Lemma 3 that when competing against deterministic adversaries, buying by the breakeven time is without loss of generality.

Proof of Lemma 3.

Fix ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), and suppose that an algorithm has simultaneous competitive ratio at most RR, so that for every y>0y>0 the target is met at one of the two horizons yy and ρ​y\rho y. Let XX denote its random buy time and let C⁡(y)=𝔼⁡[cX​(y)]C(y)=\mathbb{E}[c_{X}(y)] be its expected cost at horizon yy.

For any t≥1t\geq 1, consider the pair of horizons t/ρt/\rho and tt. The offline optimum has cost 11 at both horizons. The simultaneous guarantee therefore implies that at least one of C⁡(t/ρ)C(t/\rho) and C⁡(t)C(t) is at most RR. Moreover, the cost of every deterministic algorithm is nondecreasing in the horizon, so C⁡(t)≤C⁡(t/ρ)C(t)\leq C(t/\rho). It follows that C⁡(t)≤RC(t)\leq R for every t≥1t\geq 1.

We next consider the behavior of the algorithm on long horizons. For every realization of XX, the cost cX​(t)c_{X}(t) increases to X+1X+1 as t→∞t\to\infty, where the limit is infinite when X=∞X=\infty. Hence, by monotone convergence, 𝔼⁡[X+1]=limt→∞C⁡(t)≤R\mathbb{E}[X+1]=\lim_{t\to\infty}C(t)\leq R. In particular, the algorithm buys eventually with probability one and has finite expected buy time.

Now truncate the buy time at the breakeven point by setting X′=min⁡{X,1}X^{\prime}=\min\{X,1\}. If y<1y<1, this modification does not change the cost: realizations with X<1X<1 are unchanged, while both algorithms continue renting through horizon yy whenever X≥1X\geq 1. If y≥1y\geq 1, the truncated algorithm has expected cost 1+𝔼⁡[min⁡{X,1}]≤𝔼⁡[X+1]≤R1+\mathbb{E}[\min\{X,1\}]\leq\mathbb{E}[X+1]\leq R. Since OPT​(y)=1\mbox{OPT}(y)=1 for such horizons, its competitive ratio is at most RR.

To see that the simultaneous guarantee is preserved, consider any pair y,ρ​yy,\rho y and choose a horizon in this pair at which the original algorithm has competitive ratio at most RR. If that horizon is smaller than 11, its cost is unchanged by the truncation. If it is at least 11, the preceding bound shows directly that the truncated algorithm has competitive ratio at most RR there. Thus truncating the buy time at 11 preserves the simultaneous competitive ratio.

The same conclusion holds when the algorithm knows only that ρ≤α\rho\leq\alpha. Indeed, apply the preceding argument to any one admissible value of ρ\rho, for example ρ=α\rho=\alpha, to obtain 𝔼⁡[X+1]≤R\mathbb{E}[X+1]\leq R. The truncation argument itself is pointwise and does not depend on ρ\rho, so the resulting algorithm preserves the guarantee for every ρ≤α\rho\leq\alpha. ∎

Appendix D Proofs for the Buy-by-Breakeven-Time Tight Threshold

Section 3.6 gives the weighted tail bound (31), derives D⁡(ρ,ξ)D(\rho,\xi) in (34), and shows the general form of the positive construction in Lemma 10. This appendix shows that these ingredients can be put together to obtain a tight threshold for algorithms that buy by the breakeven time.

Recall that fixing a target competitive ratio below RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}} gives a residual curve AA that satisfies the two-scale inequality (23) for some γ>0\gamma>0, while Lemma 1 requires ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0. Since both the cost curve and the offline optimum are constant after time 11, there is a number a=A⁡(1)a=A(1) such that A⁡(y)=aA(y)=a for every y≥1y\geq 1. Applying (23) at any y≥1/ρy\geq 1/\rho gives (1+γ)​a≤0(1+\gamma)a\leq 0, and hence

A⁡(y)=A⁡(1)=a≤0for every ​y≥1.A(y)=A(1)=a\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }y\geq 1. (74)

Then both the positive and negative results reduce to the behavior of D⁡(ρ,ξ)D(\rho,\xi). The analytic bounds below determine when D⁡(ρ,ξ)≤1D(\rho,\xi)\leq 1 for every admissible ξ\xi, which yields impossibility, and when D⁡(ρ,ξ)>1D(\rho,\xi)>1 for some ξ<1\xi<1, which gives a positive construction by applying Lemma 10 with the constant tail g=−1g=-1.

D.1 Analytic bounds

We first extend the analytic results from Lemma 9. Recall in (29), we define the function Uρ,ξU_{\rho,\xi} as

Uρ,ξ​(t):=∑k=0∞(−ξ)k​e−t​ρk.U_{\rho,\xi}(t):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-\xi)^{k}e^{-t\rho^{k}}.

We first need the following alternate power series representation for Uρ,ξ​(t)U_{\rho,\xi}(t) All results in this paper which are verified in Lean concern various analytic properties of Uρ,ξ​(t)U_{\rho,\xi}(t) and related functions; hence, they all use this representation as an axiom.

Lemma 18 (Power-series representation).

For 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, 0≤ξ≤10\leq\xi\leq 1, and t≥0t\geq 0, we have

Uρ,ξ​(t)=∑n=0∞(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn).U_{\rho,\xi}(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}. (75)
Proof.

First suppose 0≤ξ<10\leq\xi<1. By (29), Uρ,ξ​(t)=∑j≥0(−ξ)j​e−t​ρjU_{\rho,\xi}(t)=\sum_{j\geq 0}(-\xi)^{j}e^{-t\rho^{j}}. Expanding each exponential produces terms (−ξ)j​(−t)n​ρj​n/n!(-\xi)^{j}(-t)^{n}\rho^{jn}/n!. Before exchanging the two sums, we check their absolute convergence. Since 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and t≥0t\geq 0,

∑j=0∞∑n=0∞|(−ξ)j​(−t)n​ρj​nn!|\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left|\frac{(-\xi)^{j}(-t)^{n}\rho^{jn}}{n!}\right| =∑j=0∞ξj​∑n=0∞(t​ρj)nn!=∑j=0∞ξj​et​ρj≤et​∑j=0∞ξj=et1−ξ<∞.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\xi^{j}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(t\rho^{j})^{n}}{n!}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\xi^{j}e^{t\rho^{j}}\leq e^{t}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\xi^{j}=\frac{e^{t}}{1-\xi}<\infty.

Therefore, the order of summation may be exchanged. We obtain

Uρ,ξ​(t)=∑j=0∞(−ξ)j​∑n=0∞(−t)n​ρj​nn!=∑n=0∞(−t)nn!​∑j=0∞(−ξ​ρn)j=∑n=0∞(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn).\displaystyle U_{\rho,\xi}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(-\xi)^{j}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}\rho^{jn}}{n!}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(-\xi\rho^{n})^{j}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}.

The last equality uses |ξ​ρn|<1|\xi\rho^{n}|<1, so the inner sum is a geometric series with value 1/(1+ξ​ρn)1/(1+\xi\rho^{n}).

It remains to pass to ξ=1\xi=1. From the probabilistic definition, Uρ,ξ​(t)=𝔼⁡[(−ξ)Kρ,t1+ξ].U_{\rho,\xi}(t)=\E\!\left[\frac{(-\xi)^{K_{\rho,t}}}{1+\xi}\right]. The random variable Kρ,tK_{\rho,t} is finite almost surely, and the integrand converges pointwise to (−1)Kρ,t/2(-1)^{K_{\rho,t}}/2 as ξ↑1\xi\uparrow 1. Its absolute value is at most 11 for every 0≤ξ≤10\leq\xi\leq 1. Dominated convergence therefore gives limξ↑1Uρ,ξ​(t)=Uρ,1​(t)\lim_{\xi\uparrow 1}U_{\rho,\xi}(t)=U_{\rho,1}(t).

On the series side, for 0≤ξ≤10\leq\xi\leq 1 the absolute value of the nnth term is at most tn/n!t^{n}/n!, independently of ξ\xi, and ∑n≥0tn/n!=et\sum_{n\geq 0}t^{n}/n!=e^{t}. Hence the series converges uniformly in ξ∈[0,1]\xi\in[0,1], and its limit as ξ↑1\xi\uparrow 1 is obtained by setting ξ=1\xi=1 in every term. Taking limits in the identity already proved for ξ<1\xi<1 establishes (75) at ξ=1\xi=1 as well. ∎

Our main analytic lemma is now the following, and it extends the first and second inequalities in Lemma 9 to all ρ\rho. This lemma is not specific to buy-by-breakeven time algorithms, and will also be extended and used for the impossibility proofs for general algorithms in the next section.

Lemma 19 (Buy-by-breakeven threshold bound).

For 0.31≤ρ<10.31\leq\rho<1, the function D⁡(ρ,ξ)D(\rho,\xi) is continuous in ξ∈[0,1]\xi\in[0,1]. For every ξ,t∈[0,1]\xi,t\in[0,1], we have Uρ,ξ​(t)≥0U_{\rho,\xi}(t)\geq 0 and D⁡(ρ,ξ)≤D⁡(ρ,1)D(\rho,\xi)\leq D(\rho,1). The equation D⁡(ρ,1)=1D(\rho,1)=1 has a unique solution in [0.31,0.32][0.31,0.32], with

ρ⋆≈0.311,\rho_{\star}\approx 0.311, (76)

and, for 0.31≤ρ<10.31\leq\rho<1,

D⁡(ρ,1)​{>1,0.31≤ρ<ρ⋆,=1,ρ=ρ⋆,<1,ρ>ρ⋆.D(\rho,1)\begin{cases}>1,&0.31\leq\rho<\rho_{\star},\\ =1,&\rho=\rho_{\star},\\ <1,&\rho>\rho_{\star}.\end{cases}

Proof.

Appendix F.1 gives a complete Lean proof. ∎

A technical issue is that Lemma 19 begins at ρ=0.31\rho=0.31, while the positive construction also needs the sign of D⁡(ρ,1)−1D(\rho,1)-1 for smaller ρ\rho. The following auxiliary bound supplies that range.

Lemma 20 (The lower-ρ\rho bridge).

For every 0<ρ≤31/1000<\rho\leq 31/100, we have D⁡(ρ,1)>1D(\rho,1)>1.

Lean-verified: The complete statement of this lemma; see Appendix F.2.

Proof.

Appendix F.2 certifies this lemma directly from the factorial series for D⁡(ρ,1)D(\rho,1). ∎

We finally need the following continuity result.

Lemma 21 (Continuity of DD in ξ\xi).

For every fixed 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, the function ξ↦D⁡(ρ,ξ)\xi\mapsto D(\rho,\xi) is continuous on [0,1][0,1].

Proof.

Fix 0<ρ<10<\rho<1. For x,ξ∈[0,1]x,\xi\in[0,1], the terms in (75) satisfy

|(−x)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)|≤1n!.\left|\frac{(-x)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}\right|\leq\frac{1}{n!}.

Since ∑n=0∞1/n!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}1/n! converges, the Weierstrass MM-test shows that the series defining Uρ,ξ​(x)U_{\rho,\xi}(x) converges uniformly on [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]\times[0,1]. Each term is continuous in (x,ξ)(x,\xi), so Uρ,ξ​(x)U_{\rho,\xi}(x) is jointly continuous there. It follows from (34) that ξ↦D⁡(ρ,ξ)\xi\mapsto D(\rho,\xi) is continuous on [0,1][0,1]. ∎

D.2 Proof of Theorem 4

With the above analytic results in place, the proof is now simple.

Proof.

Negative direction. Suppose ρ≥ρ⋆\rho\geq\rho_{\star}, and suppose that an improving algorithm exists. As above, there is a function AA with ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0 satisfying (23) and (74) for some γ>0\gamma>0. If γ≤ρ\gamma\leq\rho, the direct charging argument in Claim 2 gives ℒ⁡(A)≤0\mathcal{L}(A)\leq 0, a contradiction. Hence assume γ>ρ\gamma>\rho and let ξ=ρ/γ\xi=\rho/\gamma. Since ρ≥ρ⋆>0.31\rho\geq\rho_{\star}>0.31, Lemma 19 gives both Uρ,ξ​(t)≥0U_{\rho,\xi}(t)\geq 0 on [0,1][0,1] and D⁡(ρ,ξ)≤D⁡(ρ,1)≤1D(\rho,\xi)\leq D(\rho,1)\leq 1. The first conclusion verifies the remaining sign hypothesis of Lemma 8. The tail is constant with value a=A⁡(1)a=A(1), so that

ℒ⁡(A)≤a⁡(1−D⁡(ρ,ξ)).\mathcal{L}(A)\leq a\bigl(1-D(\rho,\xi)\bigr). (77)

The second conclusion gives 1−D⁡(ρ,ξ)≥01-D(\rho,\xi)\geq 0. Since A⁡(1)≤0A(1)\leq 0, (77) gives ℒ⁡(A)≤0\mathcal{L}(A)\leq 0, contradicting the necessary condition ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0.

Positive direction. Now suppose ρ<ρ⋆\rho<\rho_{\star}. If ρ≤31/100\rho\leq 31/100, then Lemma 20 gives D⁡(ρ,1)>1D(\rho,1)>1; otherwise the same conclusion follows from Lemma 19. By Lemma 21, choose 0<ξ<10<\xi<1 sufficiently close to 11 that D⁡(ρ,ξ)>1D(\rho,\xi)>1, and put γ:=ρ/ξ>ρ\gamma:=\rho/\xi>\rho.

Apply Lemma 10 with the constant function g⁡(y)=−1g(y)=-1. Its hypotheses hold because g⁡(y)+γ​g​(ρ​y)=−(1+γ)g(y)+\gamma g(\rho y)=-(1+\gamma). Set T:=1/ρT:=1/\rho. For the resulting functions ANA_{N}, (41) gives

limN→∞N​ evenℒ⁡(AN)e=−∫1TUρ,ξ(y)dy−e−T.\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\to\infty\\ N\text{ even}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mathcal{L}(A_{N})}{e}=-\int_{1}^{T}U_{\rho,\xi}(y)\,dy-e^{-T}.

To evaluate the right-hand side, integrate the recurrence (30) over [1,T][1,T]. This gives

∫1TUρ,ξ​(y)​𝑑y+ξ​∫1TUρ,ξ​(ρ​y)​𝑑y=e−1−e−T.\int_{1}^{T}U_{\rho,\xi}(y)\,dy+\xi\int_{1}^{T}U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y)\,dy=e^{-1}-e^{-T}.

In the second integral, the substitution x=ρ​yx=\rho y gives

ξ​∫1TUρ,ξ​(ρ​y)​𝑑y=ξρ​∫ρ1Uρ,ξ​(x)​𝑑x=D⁡(ρ,ξ)e,\xi\int_{1}^{T}U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho y)\,dy=\frac{\xi}{\rho}\int_{\rho}^{1}U_{\rho,\xi}(x)\,dx=\frac{D(\rho,\xi)}{e},

where the last equality follows from (34). Therefore

−∫1TUρ,ξ(y)dy−e−T=D⁡(ρ,ξ)−1e.-\int_{1}^{T}U_{\rho,\xi}(y)\,dy-e^{-T}=\frac{D(\rho,\xi)-1}{e}.

Combining the preceding identities yields

limN→∞N​ evenℒ⁡(AN)=D⁡(ρ,ξ)−1>0.\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\to\infty\\ N\text{ even}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{L}(A_{N})=D(\rho,\xi)-1>0.

Thus ℒ⁡(AN)>0\mathcal{L}(A_{N})>0 for some even NN. This is the construction in Lemma 10, started from the constant tail required by a buy-by-breakeven-time algorithm.

Applying Lemma 17 with sufficiently small smoothing intervals, followed by Lemmas 2 and 5, gives the required buy-by-breakeven-time algorithm with a simultaneous improvement over RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}. ∎

Appendix E Proofs for the Arbitrary-Algorithm Tight Threshold

Appendix D gives the tight analysis for algorithms that buy by the breakeven time. We now allow arbitrary buying times. The new work concerns the possible shapes of the residual AA after time 11, since the algorithm can now buy after the breakeven time. This renders the proof much more intricate than the previous section, though we reuse several ideas from there.

We proceed in three steps. First, we express the tail of an arbitrary algorithm in terms of its buying time; this is a piecewise linear function leading to the shape of the residual curve in Figure 4. Second, we evaluate its contribution to the weighted integral ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A). This introduces hρ,ξ​(τ)h_{\rho,\xi}(\tau), which measures the contribution of buying at time τ\tau. We then show that the sign of this function is controlled by its value at T=1/ρT=1/\rho. The scaled value at this point is the function K⁡(ρ,ξ)K(\rho,\xi) that determines the threshold ρ\rho value between possibility and impossibility. Finally, we determine when KK changes sign. The positive direction then uses the recursive extension from Lemma 10 and realization lemmas from Appendix B to complete the proof.

For a target ratio R<RskiR<R_{\mathrm{ski}}, the residual curve is A=CF−R​OPT=AF,ηA=C_{F}-R\mbox{OPT}=A_{F,\eta}. The quantities below depend instead on ρ\rho and ξ\xi assuming η=Rski−R\eta=R_{\mathrm{ski}}-R is given, and further assume η\eta is fixed. We retain the functions Uρ,ξU_{\rho,\xi} and D⁡(ρ,ξ)D(\rho,\xi) from Appendix D. Recall that ℒ⁡(A)=e​∫0∞A⁡(y)​e−y​𝑑y\mathcal{L}(A)=e\int_{0}^{\infty}A(y)e^{-y}\,dy. By Lemma 1, an improvement over RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}} requires ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0.

E.1 Reducing ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) via the weighted cost hρ,ξh_{\rho,\xi}

This subsection rewrites the bound on ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) from Lemma 8 in terms of the buying time XX. The function sτ​(y)s_{\tau}(y) is the part of the eventual cost of buying at time τ\tau that has yet to be paid at horizon yy. The weight Wρ,ξW_{\rho,\xi} combines the two integrals in the bound, and hρ,ξ​(τ)h_{\rho,\xi}(\tau) is the weighted contribution of sτs_{\tau}. These quantities give the bound on ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) in (81). This bound combines a constant term from the previous section (buying by breakeven time) and a second term encoded by hρ,ξ​(τ)h_{\rho,\xi}(\tau) that captures buying at later time points.

We first describe the part of a residual curve that comes from buying after time 11. For τ≥0\tau\geq 0 and y≥1y\geq 1, set

sτ​(y):={τ+1−y,y<τ,0,y≥τ.s_{\tau}(y):=\begin{cases}\tau+1-y,&y<\tau,\\ 0,&y\geq\tau.\end{cases}

As we show below, sτ​(y)s_{\tau}(y) is the difference between the eventual cost τ+1\tau+1 of buying at time τ\tau and the cost at horizon yy.

Let XX be the buying time of an algorithm with residual curve A=CF−R​OPTA=C_{F}-R\mbox{OPT}, where R<RskiR<R_{\mathrm{ski}}, and suppose that AA satisfies (23). Then 𝔼⁡[X]<∞\mathbb{E}[X]<\infty. Set A∞:=𝔼⁡[X+1]−RA_{\infty}:=\mathbb{E}[X+1]-R. Then A∞≤0A_{\infty}\leq 0, and, for every y≥1y\geq 1,

A(y)=A∞−𝔼[𝟏{X>1}sX(y)].A(y)=A_{\infty}-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{X>1\}}s_{X}(y)\right]. (78)

Set η:=Rski−R\eta:=R_{\mathrm{ski}}-R, so that A=CF−R​OPT=AF,ηA=C_{F}-R\mbox{OPT}=A_{F,\eta}. Since AA satisfies (23), Lemma 5 shows that FF has simultaneous distributional competitive ratio at most RR. Lemma 6 therefore shows that the algorithm buys eventually almost surely,

cτ​(y)={y,y<τ,τ+1,y≥τ.c_{\tau}(y)=\begin{cases}y,&y<\tau,\\ \tau+1,&y\geq\tau.\end{cases}

cτ​(y)−(τ+1)={y−τ−1,y<τ,0,y≥τ,=−sτ​(y).c_{\tau}(y)-(\tau+1)=\begin{cases}y-\tau-1,&y<\tau,\\ 0,&y\geq\tau,\end{cases}=-s_{\tau}(y).

sτ(y)=𝟏{τ>1}sτ(y)(y≥1).s_{\tau}(y)=\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau>1\}}s_{\tau}(y)\qquad(y\geq 1).

A⁡(y)\displaystyle A(y) =CF​(y)−R\displaystyle=C_{F}(y)-R

=A∞−𝔼[𝟏{X>1}sX(y)].\displaystyle=A_{\infty}-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{X>1\}}s_{X}(y)\right].

The expectations are finite because Lemma 6 gives 𝔼⁡[X+1]<∞\mathbb{E}[X+1]<\infty, while 0≤sX​(y)≤X+10\leq s_{X}(y)\leq X+1. This proves (78). ∎

Lemma 8 bounds ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) by two integrals over [1,1/ρ][1,1/\rho] and [1/ρ,∞)[1/\rho,\infty). We combine them by defining

Wρ,ξ​(y):={Uρ,ξ​(y),1≤y<1/ρ,e−y,y≥1/ρ.W_{\rho,\xi}(y):=\begin{cases}U_{\rho,\xi}(y),&1\leq y<1/\rho,\\[2.84526pt] e^{-y},&y\geq 1/\rho.\end{cases} (79)

For 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and 0≤ξ≤10\leq\xi\leq 1,

Lemma 24 (Weighted tail decomposition).

Under the assumptions of Lemma 22, suppose also that 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, γ>ρ\gamma>\rho, ξ=ρ/γ\xi=\rho/\gamma, and Uρ,ξ​(t)≥0U_{\rho,\xi}(t)\geq 0 for 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1. Then

E.2 Non-negativity of the weighted cost hρ,ξh_{\rho,\xi}

In order to show an impossibility result, we need to show ℒ⁡(A)≤0\mathcal{L}(A)\leq 0. Equation (81) shows that this happens when hρ,ξ​(τ)≥0h_{\rho,\xi}(\tau)\geq 0 for every possible buying time τ≥1\tau\geq 1. We begin with a property of Uρ,ξU_{\rho,\xi} that will imply concavity of hρ,ξh_{\rho,\xi}. We then calculate hρ,ξh_{\rho,\xi} at 11 and at T:=1/ρT:=1/\rho, the point where the definition of Wρ,ξW_{\rho,\xi} changes, and study its shape on either side of TT. Finally, we introduce K⁡(ρ,ξ)K(\rho,\xi) as a series expression for the scaled value of hρ,ξ​(T)h_{\rho,\xi}(T), and reduce the sign condition to a condition on the sign of K⁡(ρ,ξ)K(\rho,\xi). These facts together determine the sign of hρ,ξ​(τ)h_{\rho,\xi}(\tau) for every τ≥1\tau\geq 1.

E.4 Proof of Theorem 5

The proof now follows the sign of K⁡(ρ,ξ)K(\rho,\xi), which by (89) is the sign of the contribution from buying at T=1/ρT=1/\rho. In the range used for the impossibility result, D⁡(ρ,ξ)≤1D(\rho,\xi)\leq 1. If K⁡(ρ,ξ)≥0K(\rho,\xi)\geq 0, then Corollary 4 shows that every buying time τ≥1\tau\geq 1 has hρ,ξ​(τ)≥0h_{\rho,\xi}(\tau)\geq 0. The weighted decomposition in Lemma 24 then shows that no distribution over late buying times can make ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) positive.

If K⁡(ρ,ξ)<0K(\rho,\xi)<0, the buying time TT itself has hρ,ξ​(T)<0h_{\rho,\xi}(T)<0. The construction below starts from the tail g=−sTg=-s_{T} and extends it recursively to earlier times. For the resulting curves, the weighted integral ℒ⁡(AN)\mathcal{L}(A_{N}) approaches a positive limit. The realization lemmas then turn one of these curves into an algorithm. Thus the sign of the contribution from buying at the transition time TT both rules out an improvement on one side of the threshold and provides the construction on the other. We now formalize this.

Proof.

We again prove the negative direction first. Suppose ρ≥ρall\rho\geq\rho_{\mathrm{all}} and an improving algorithm exists. Its residual curve satisfies (23) for some γ>0\gamma>0, together with ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0. Lemma 6 gives A⁡(y)≤0A(y)\leq 0 for y≥1y\geq 1.

If γ≤ρ\gamma\leq\rho, the direct charging argument in Claim 2 gives ℒ⁡(A)≤0\mathcal{L}(A)\leq 0. That argument uses only the sign of the tail. Hence assume γ>ρ\gamma>\rho and put ξ=ρ/γ\xi=\rho/\gamma. Because ρ≥ρall>1/3>ρ⋆>31/100\rho\geq\rho_{\mathrm{all}}>1/3>\rho_{\star}>31/100, Lemma 19 gives both Uρ,ξ​(t)≥0U_{\rho,\xi}(t)\geq 0 on [0,1][0,1] and D⁡(ρ,ξ)≤D⁡(ρ,1)≤1D(\rho,\xi)\leq D(\rho,1)\leq 1. Lemmas 29 and 30 also give

K⁡(ρ,ξ)≥K⁡(ρ,1)≥K⁡(ρall,1)=0.K(\rho,\xi)\geq K(\rho,1)\geq K(\rho_{\mathrm{all}},1)=0.

Lemma 28 now gives ℒ⁡(A)≤0\mathcal{L}(A)\leq 0, contradicting ℒ⁡(A)>0\mathcal{L}(A)>0.

Positive direction.

Now suppose ρ<ρall\rho<\rho_{\mathrm{all}}. Lemma 30 gives K⁡(ρ,1)<0K(\rho,1)<0. By the continuity in Lemma 29, choose ξ<1\xi<1 sufficiently close to 11 that K⁡(ρ,ξ)<0K(\rho,\xi)<0, and put γ:=ρ/ξ>ρ\gamma:=\rho/\xi>\rho.

Let T:=1/ρT:=1/\rho and take the function

g⁡(y):={y−T−1,1≤y<T,0,y≥T.g(y):=\begin{cases}y-T-1,&1\leq y<T,\\ 0,&y\geq T.\end{cases}

This function is nonpositive on [1,T)[1,T). If T≤y<T/ρT\leq y<T/\rho, then g⁡(y)=0g(y)=0 and g⁡(ρ​y)≤0g(\rho y)\leq 0; if y≥T/ρy\geq T/\rho, both terms vanish. Thus gg satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 10. For the resulting functions ANA_{N}, that lemma gives the two-scale inequality (23) and

limN→∞N​ evenℒ⁡(AN)e=∫1Tg⁡(z)​Uρ,ξ​(z)​𝑑z=−1−ρρ2​K​(ρ,ξ)>0.\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\to\infty\\ N\text{ even}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mathcal{L}(A_{N})}{e}=\int_{1}^{T}g(z)U_{\rho,\xi}(z)\,dz=-\frac{1-\rho}{\rho^{2}}K(\rho,\xi)>0.

Indeed, g⁡(z)=−(T+1−z)g(z)=-(T+1-z) on [1,T][1,T], while Wρ,ξ​(z)=Uρ,ξ​(z)W_{\rho,\xi}(z)=U_{\rho,\xi}(z) there. Hence, by the definition of hρ,ξh_{\rho,\xi} and (89),

∫1Tg⁡(z)​Uρ,ξ​(z)​𝑑z=−hρ,ξ​(T)=−1−ρρ2​K​(ρ,ξ).\int_{1}^{T}g(z)U_{\rho,\xi}(z)\,dz=-h_{\rho,\xi}(T)=-\frac{1-\rho}{\rho^{2}}K(\rho,\xi).

Hence ℒ⁡(AN)>0\mathcal{L}(A_{N})>0 for some even NN. This is exactly the construction in Lemma 10, with T=1/ρT=1/\rho.

Applying Lemma 17, followed by Lemmas 16, 2, and 5, gives an algorithm with a strict simultaneous improvement over RskiR_{\mathrm{ski}}. ∎

Finally, to solve K⁡(ρ,1)=0K(\rho,1)=0, numerical bisection gives ρall≈0.338\rho_{\mathrm{all}}\approx 0.338.

Appendix F Lean Proofs

The Lean code is available at https://github.com/relyt871/BWCA-Online-Lean. The lean/ directory of this repository contains a standalone Lean project. Build instructions are given in the repository’s root README.md. All file paths below are relative to the repository root.

Some finite rational computations are checked using Lean’s native_decide tactic. Every such application concerns an explicit rational equality or inequality, a finite partial sum, or positivity of a finite list or table of coefficients. The surrounding analytic reductions are expressed as ordinary Lean proofs. These computations use exact arithmetic and rely on Lean’s native compiler in addition to its kernel; their generated axiom dependencies can be inspected with #print axioms.

All results in this paper which are verified in Lean concern analytic properties of the power series representation (Eq.(75)) of Uρ,ξ​(t)U_{\rho,\xi}(t) given in Lemma 18: for ρ∈(0,1),ξ∈[0,1]\rho\in(0,1),\xi\in[0,1], and t≥0t\geq 0:

Uρ,ξ​(t)=∑n=0∞(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn).U_{\rho,\xi}(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}.

F.1 Lean certificates for Lemma 19

This appendix explains the Lean certificates used in Lemma 19. The entry point is:

lean/buy_by_breakeven_threshold/BuyByBreakevenRho.lean
1. The endpoint-safe definition of UU.

The expression from Lemma 18 is encoded as Upower

theorem buy_by_breakeven_U_power_series (rho xi t : Real) :
    U rho xi t = sum’ n,
      (-t)^n / ((Nat.factorial n : Real) * (1 + xi * rho^n))
2. The functional identity.

Lean proves the identity

Uρ,ξ​(t)+ξ​Uρ,ξ​(ρ​t)=e−tU_{\rho,\xi}(t)+\xi U_{\rho,\xi}(\rho t)=e^{-t}

directly from the power series. The proof is coefficientwise: for each nn,

(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)+ξ​(−ρ​t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)=(−t)nn!.\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}+\xi\frac{(-\rho t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}=\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!}.

Summing this identity gives:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_U_functional_identity {rho xi t : Real}
    (hrho0 : 0 <= rho) (hxi0 : 0 <= xi) :
    U rho xi t + xi * U rho xi (rho * t) = Real.exp (-t)
3. The dual multiplier recurrence.

Lean defines the orbit weight and multiplier by

buyByBreakevenOrbitWeight rho x k
buyByBreakevenMultiplier rho gamma x k

corresponding to

bk​(x)=ρk​e−ρk​x,uk​(x)=ρkγ​Uρ,ρ/γ​(ρk​x).b_{k}(x)=\rho^{k}e^{-\rho^{k}x},\qquad u_{k}(x)=\frac{\rho^{k}}{\gamma}U_{\rho,\rho/\gamma}(\rho^{k}x).

Using the functional identity and elementary algebra, Lean proves:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_multiplier_recurrence {rho gamma x : Real}
    (hrho0 : 0 <= rho) (hgamma : 0 < gamma) (k : Nat) :
    gamma * buyByBreakevenMultiplier rho gamma x k
      + buyByBreakevenMultiplier rho gamma x (k + 1)
      = buyByBreakevenOrbitWeight rho x k

This is the recurrence γ​uk+uk+1=bk\gamma u_{k}+u_{k+1}=b_{k} used in the dual certificate.

4. Nonnegative multipliers.

The paper proves the sign of UU from the geometric crossing representation in Lemma 7. Lean also supplies an independent algebraic verification. It proves

theorem buy_by_breakeven_U_nonneg {rho xi t : Real}
    (hrho0 : (31 / 100 : Real) <= rho) (hrho1 : rho <= 1)
    (hxi0 : 0 <= xi) (hxi1 : xi <= 1)
    (ht0 : 0 <= t) (ht1 : t <= 1) :
    0 <= U rho xi t

The Lean proof keeps the first four power-series terms, proves the alternating tail is nonnegative, clears denominators in the resulting cubic lower bound, and checks exact rational Bernstein coefficients on the box ρ∈[0.31,1]\rho\in[0.31,1], ξ,t∈[0,1]\xi,t\in[0,1].

Consequently, Lean also proves nonnegativity of the actual multipliers:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_multiplier_nonneg {rho gamma x : Real}
    (hrho0 : (31 / 100 : Real) <= rho) (hrho1 : rho <= 1)
    (hgamma : 0 < gamma) (hxi1 : rho / gamma <= 1)
    (hx0 : 0 <= x) (hx1 : x <= 1) (k : Nat) :
    0 <= buyByBreakevenMultiplier rho gamma x k
5. The endpoint comparison in ξ\xi.

Lean first proves continuity on the full closed interval:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_D_continuousOn_xi {rho : Real}
    (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (hrho1 : rho <= 1) :
    ContinuousOn (fun xi => D rho xi) (Set.Icc 0 1)

The proof bounds every term uniformly by 1/n!1/n!. Lean then proves the full comparison D⁡(ρ,ξ)≤D⁡(ρ,1)D(\rho,\xi)\leq D(\rho,1). The proof first identifies the integral definition of DD with the termwise integrated power series. It differentiates this series in ξ\xi, with each derivative term bounded by a summable factorial series. The first four terms are the finite expression

1−ρ(1+ξ)2−1−ρ22​(1+ξ​ρ)2+1−ρ36​(1+ξ​ρ2)2−1−ρ424​(1+ξ​ρ3)2.\frac{1-\rho}{(1+\xi)^{2}}-\frac{1-\rho^{2}}{2(1+\xi\rho)^{2}}+\frac{1-\rho^{3}}{6(1+\xi\rho^{2})^{2}}-\frac{1-\rho^{4}}{24(1+\xi\rho^{3})^{2}}.

Lean certifies this finite expression:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_Dxi_finite_nonneg {rho xi : Real}
    (hrho0 : (31 / 100 : Real) <= rho) (hrho1 : rho <= 1)
    (hxi0 : 0 <= xi) (hxi1 : xi <= 1) :
    0 <= buyByBreakevenDxiFinite rho xi

The proof clears positive denominators and checks exact rational Bernstein coefficients on the square ρ∈[0.31,1]\rho\in[0.31,1], ξ∈[0,1]\xi\in[0,1]. It also proves that the magnitudes of the remaining terms decrease, so the alternating tail beginning with its positive term is nonnegative. These two facts make the full derivative nonnegative. The derivative test then gives the endpoint comparison:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_D_le_endpoint {rho xi : Real}
    (hrho0 : (31 / 100 : Real) <= rho) (hrho1 : rho <= 1)
    (hxi0 : 0 <= xi) (hxi1 : xi <= 1) :
    D rho xi <= D rho 1

The case ξ=0\xi=0 follows directly from the integral definition and the certified nonnegativity of Uρ,1U_{\rho,1}. For ξ>0\xi>0, Lean applies the derivative argument on the interval [ξ,1][\xi,1].

6. Strict decrease in ρ\rho.

The entry file also formalizes the one-variable argument for D⁡(ρ,1)D(\rho,1). It identifies DD with its factorially convergent series and differentiates that series term by term on every neighborhood contained in (0,1)(0,1). Consecutive derivative terms are then paired. The first pair is zero, while every later pair is strictly negative. Summability makes this pairing valid for the infinite series. Lean concludes:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_D_strictAntiOn_rho :
    StrictAntiOn (fun rho : Real => D rho 1) (Set.Ioo 0 1)
7. Existence and uniqueness of ρ⋆\rho_{\star}.

Lean proves that the magnitudes in the alternating series for D⁡(ρ,1)D(\rho,1) decrease throughout 0≤ρ≤10\leq\rho\leq 1. Even and odd finite sums therefore give rigorous lower and upper bounds. It combines these bounds with Mathlib’s enclosure of ee and exact rational arithmetic to prove opposite signs at two rational points whose interval rounds to 0.3110.311. Continuity gives a root, and the strict decrease above makes it unique. The paper’s three-decimal value is captured by:

theorem buy_by_breakeven_rho_star_eq :
    D buyByBreakevenRhoStar 1 = 1

theorem buy_by_breakeven_rho_star_rounds_to_0311 :
    |buyByBreakevenRhoStar - (311 / 1000 : Real)| < 1 / 2000

Finally, the same monotonicity theorem proves D⁡(ρ,1)>1D(\rho,1)>1 below this root and D⁡(ρ,1)<1D(\rho,1)<1 above it. Thus Lean verifies every assertion in Lemma 19.

F.3 Lean certificates for Lemma 25

This subsection explains the Lean check for the sign estimate in Lemma 25.

The formal statement proves directly that Uρ,ξ​(t)+ρ​Uρ,ξ′​(t)≥0U_{\rho,\xi}(t)+\rho U^{\prime}_{\rho,\xi}(t)\geq 0 when ρ∈[1/3,1]\rho\in[1/3,1] and ξ,t∈[0,1]\xi,t\in[0,1]. The Lean proof uses the power-series representation

Uρ,ξ​(t)=∑n=0∞(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn).U_{\rho,\xi}(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}.

This is called Upower in the formalization. The paper-facing theorem is part of the general-KK analytic file:

lean/general_K/GeneralKAnalytic.lean

theorem general_endpoint_concavity_factor_nonneg {rho xi t : Real}
    (hrho0 : (1 / 3 : Real) <= rho) (hrho1 : rho <= 1)

Its proof has three parts.

1. The expression checked by Lean.

Lean first defines the individual terms in the power series:

noncomputable def Upower (rho xi t : Real) : Real :=
  sum’ n, (-t)^n / ((Nat.factorial n : Real) *
    (1 + xi * rho^n))

The displayed Lean statements use ASCII notation for mathematical symbols.

2. Rewriting U+ρ​U′U+\rho U^{\prime} as the series in the paper.

Lean proves that the power series can be differentiated term by term on the interval needed in the paper. The main theorem for this step is hasDerivAt_Upower. It uses a uniform bound by a factorial series on the open interval (−1,2)(-1,2), which contains all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. After differentiating, Lean proves that the derivative series is the shifted series:

theorem UpowerDerivSeries_eq_neg_shifted <omitted parameters>:
    UpowerDerivSeries rho xi t
      = - sum’ n, UpowerShiftTerm rho xi n t

Then it checks the algebraic identity for every coefficient:

(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)−ρ​(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn+1)=(1−ρ)​(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)​(1+ξ​ρn+1).\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})}-\rho\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n+1})}=(1-\rho)\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})(1+\xi\rho^{n+1})}.

In Lean this per-term algebra step is named Upower_term_sub_rho_shift_eq. Together with the derivative theorem, it identifies the series with the expression U+ρ​U′U+\rho U^{\prime} used in the paper.

3. Proving the series is at least zero.

The remaining task is the series sign check on the box. Lean writes

Uρ,ξ​(t)+ρ​Uρ,ξ′​(t)1−ρ=∑n=0∞(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)​(1+ξ​ρn+1).\frac{U_{\rho,\xi}(t)+\rho U^{\prime}_{\rho,\xi}(t)}{1-\rho}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})(1+\xi\rho^{n+1})}.

It keeps the first six terms and proves that their sum is already positive. After clearing denominators, this six-term expression is a polynomial in ρ,ξ,t\rho,\xi,t. Lean substitutes

ρ=13+23​α,ξ=β,t=τ,\rho=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\alpha,\qquad\xi=\beta,\qquad t=\tau,

so that the domain becomes the unit cube (α,β,τ)∈[0,1]3(\alpha,\beta,\tau)\in[0,1]^{3}. The cleared polynomial is then expressed in the tensor-product Bernstein basis of degrees (20,5,5)(20,5,5). All Bernstein coefficients are exact rational numbers, stored in lean/SkiRental/LemmaCertificates.lean, and Lean checks that every one is positive:

theorem generalVPositiveP5TBernsteinCoeffs_positive :
    allBlocksPositive generalVPositiveP5TBernsteinCoeffs = true := by
  native_decide

The reusable lemma in lean/SkiRental/Polynomial.lean says that a Bernstein polynomial with positive coefficients is positive on the unit cube. This yields positivity of the six-term lower polynomial.

Finally, Lean verifies that the alternating tail starting at term 66 is at least zero. This uses the elementary fact that, on the same box, the magnitudes of the remaining terms are decreasing. Therefore

∑n=05(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)​(1+ξ​ρn+1)≤∑n=0∞(−t)nn!​(1+ξ​ρn)​(1+ξ​ρn+1).\sum_{n=0}^{5}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})(1+\xi\rho^{n+1})}\leq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{n}}{n!(1+\xi\rho^{n})(1+\xi\rho^{n+1})}.

The exact internal theorem names are generalVPositiveSixTerm_pos_on_box for positivity of the six-term polynomial, generalVPositiveSixTerm_le_rawSeries for the alternating-tail comparison, and generalVPositiveSeries_nonneg_on_box for the nonnegativity of the series. The paper-facing theorem above combines these facts with the termwise derivative identity. The numerical coefficients are rational numbers, and the positivity checks are exact.

Lean proves the complete statement of Lemma 30. The file GeneralKRho.lean proves the coefficient derivative bounds, justifies differentiation of the infinite series, and proves that the derivative of K⁡(ρ,1)K(\rho,1) is positive on (0,1)(0,1). Its final two theorems are:

    StrictMonoOn (fun rho : Real => K rho 1) (Set.Ioo 0 1)

The second theorem applies the intermediate value theorem to the certified endpoint signs and then uses strict increase for uniqueness. Thus Lean gives the complete proofs of Lemmas 29 and 30, together with the exact weighted identity (88).

F.5 Lean verification of Lemma 9

Lemma 9 contains three estimates for the function UU at ρ=1/3\rho=1/3. The paper obtains the first estimate from Lemma 7, and Lean supplies an independent check. The second estimate is a direct Lean theorem. Lean also checks the complete conversion of the third estimate from its integral to the alternating series. We describe each part in the order in which it appears in the lemma. The entry points are
